title: Aether Fuels Produces ASTM-Compliant Synthetic Aviation Fuel in Integrated Demonstration
description:
Aether Fuels has successfully operated a fully integrated demonstration line producing synthetic aviation fuel that meets ASTM D7566 specifications, marking a step toward commercial deployment of its Aurora sustainable aviation fuel (SAF) technology.
The system converted renewable natural gas derived from Kentucky landfill gas and captured industrial carbon dioxide into fully upgraded synthetic aviation fuel.
"This demonstration proves Aether's ability to scale up our integrated Aurora platform, take a feedstock through the complete end-to-end process, and produce on-spec synthetic aviation fuel," said Dhaval Shah, chief technology officer of Aether Fuels.
Aether projects that fuel from these facilities could achieve lifecycle greenhouse gas emissions reductions exceeding 70% compared with conventional fossil jet fuel.
Aether CEO and co-founder Conor Madigan said the integrated demonstration follows the company's earlier work validating individual components of the Aurora platform and scaling up its technology in standalone demonstration units.
text:
Aether Fuels has successfully operated a fully integrated demonstration line producing synthetic aviation fuel that meets ASTM D7566 specifications, marking a step toward commercial deployment of its Aurora sustainable aviation fuel (SAF) technology.

The demonstration, conducted at RTI International in North Carolina, combined Aether's 2.5-barrel-per-day Aurora Tri-Converter and Upgrader units with RTI's existing Fischer-Tropsch reactor. The system converted renewable natural gas derived from Kentucky landfill gas and captured industrial carbon dioxide into fully upgraded synthetic aviation fuel.

Independent testing by AmSpec confirmed that fuel samples met the applicable ASTM D7566 specifications for Fischer-Tropsch Synthesized Paraffinic Kerosene (FT-SPK). Under the standard, qualifying FT-SPK can be blended with conventional jet fuel at concentrations of up to 50% without modifications to existing aircraft or airport fueling infrastructure.

"This demonstration proves Aether's ability to scale up our integrated Aurora platform, take a feedstock through the complete end-to-end process, and produce on-spec synthetic aviation fuel," said Dhaval Shah, chief technology officer of Aether Fuels.

The demonstration builds on previous testing of Aether's standalone Tri-Converter technology and provides engineering data for the company's planned Project Beacon facility in Singapore.

Project Beacon is designed to produce approximately 2,000 metric tons of SAF annually, equivalent to 50 barrels per day. Aether said the latest demonstration will inform the facility's design and help reduce technical risks ahead of commercial deployment.

The company is also developing additional commercial projects intended to produce ASTM-compliant SAF. Aether projects that fuel from these facilities could achieve lifecycle greenhouse gas emissions reductions exceeding 70% compared with conventional fossil jet fuel.

Aether CEO and co-founder Conor Madigan said the integrated demonstration follows the company's earlier work validating individual components of the Aurora platform and scaling up its technology in standalone demonstration units.

title: Implications of Potential US Diesel Export Ban and Pressure on Europe - ResourceWise
description:
A potential US diesel export ban is becoming more than a domestic fuel-price debate.
Washington could use a potential diesel export ban to pressure France and Germany into releasing emergency stocks.
Lower diesel prices could squeeze soybean oil-based biofuel margins and prompt adjustments in D4 RIN prices.
Why Is a US Diesel Export Ban Being Discussed?
US diesel exports in June were 12% higher than in January, while jet fuel exports rose approximately 25% over the same period.
text:
A potential US diesel export ban is becoming more than a domestic fuel-price debate. It could also become a bargaining chip to pressure Europe into releasing emergency supplies.

Reuters reported that the Trump administration has told France and Germany to draw down emergency diesel inventories to help ease global fuel prices or face a possible US export ban.

The immediate appeal is straightforward: keep more American diesel at home or persuade European governments to put additional barrels into circulation. Either approach could offer relief in a tight market.

But a recent Prima CarbonZero analyst report highlights why restricting exports could produce consequences that extend well beyond diesel. An initial price decline could weaken refinery economics, reduce production of other fuels, and change the balance between fossil diesel, renewable fuels, and compliance credits.

Key Takeaways

The export threat could provide leverage. Washington could use a potential diesel export ban to pressure France and Germany into releasing emergency stocks.

Domestic price relief could be temporary. As storage fills and margins weaken, refiners could cut output, tightening gasoline and jet fuel supplies.

Biofuel economics could shift. Lower diesel prices could squeeze soybean oil-based biofuel margins and prompt adjustments in D4 RIN prices.

Policy details will shape the impact. European stock releases, the potential ban’s scope and duration, and refinery responses will determine whether intervention eases pressure or creates new constraints.

Why Is a US Diesel Export Ban Being Discussed?

Strong domestic demand, high exports, and low inventories have put diesel prices under pressure. This holds true even as refiners run hard to capture attractive margins.

According to a Prima CarbonZero analysis, reduced global middle distillate supply associated with conflict in the Middle East has increased demand for US exports. US diesel exports in June were 12% higher than in January, while jet fuel exports rose approximately 25% over the same period.

Those international supply pressures are colliding with domestic concerns about fuel affordability, particularly among farmers.

Could the Threat Encourage France and Germany to Release Stocks?

The potential leverage comes from the consequences of losing access to US diesel exports. In an already constrained international market, removing those barrels could intensify competition for replacement supplies.

Releasing emergency diesel stocks could help ease that pressure while giving Washington an alternative to restricting exports. In this scenario, the threat functions as a negotiating tool intended to bring additional supply into the market.

However, a stock release and an export ban work differently. A release makes stored fuel available for consumption. A ban initially redirects existing US production toward the domestic market, with the eventual outcome depending on storage capacity and refiners’ willingness to maintain output.

Emergency stocks also provide a temporary buffer. They cannot indefinitely compensate for disrupted supply or insufficient production.

The central concern comes down to whether diplomatic pressure can secure meaningful near-term relief and whether that relief can bridge the market to more sustainable supply conditions.

Why Might Domestic Price Relief Be Short-Lived?

Keeping export barrels in the United States could initially increase domestic availability and push diesel prices lower. But the Prima CarbonZero report identifies a limit to that benefit: spare storage capacity.

Once refiners lose access to overseas buyers, surplus diesel must find a domestic customer or be stored. As storage fills and diesel margins weaken, refiners could reduce processing rates.

That response would affect more than diesel. Refineries produce multiple fuels, so lower utilization could also reduce gasoline and jet fuel supply.

The American Fuel & Petrochemical Manufacturers warns that restricting diesel exports could consequently raise prices for those products. The group also points to the approaching home heating oil season as a particularly difficult time to constrain refinery output.

Lifting a temporary ban could create another adjustment. Domestic diesel prices would reconnect with a potentially tighter international market, exposing buyers to a renewed price increase.

A policy intended to provide immediate relief could therefore exchange today's price pressure for production cuts and volatility later.

What Would This Mean for Renewable Diesel and Biodiesel?

The implications would extend into biofuel margins and compliance markets.

The relationship between soybean oil and heating oil prices is a key transmission channel. If a ban pushed domestic diesel and heating oil prices lower while soybean oil remained relatively expensive, the feedstock-to-fuel balance could become less favorable for soybean oil-based biofuel production.

The Prima CarbonZero analyst report suggests that D4 Renewable Identification Number prices would need to respond to help rebalance biofuel economics. The size and timing of that adjustment would depend on the broader market response.

For biofuel participants, the relevant signal is therefore the interaction among fuel prices, feedstock costs, refinery output, and compliance credits.

What Should Fuel Market Participants Watch?

The most consequential outcome may be whether the export threat prompts European stock releases without becoming an enacted restriction.

If a ban does proceed, its scope and duration will matter alongside storage availability, refinery utilization, and movements in fuel and credit prices.

A measure aimed at lowering the price of one fuel can reshape production and the economy across several connected markets. Understanding those relationships will be essential to assessing whether any intervention offers lasting relief or simply moves the pressure elsewhere.

Put Policy Headlines Into a Broader Biofuels Market Context

The diesel export debate illustrates how policy decisions can ripple through fuel prices, feedstock demand, and biofuel margins. Understanding those connections is essential to assessing your next commercial move.

title: Dongde Energy starts $1.6-B eSAF project in China - Hydrocarbon Processing

Dongde Energy has begun implementing a $1.6-B sustainable aviation fuel (SAF) project in Xinjiang, China, which will use green hydrogen and captured CO₂ to produce 100,000 tpy of SAF.
The project in Yiwu county will capture and utilize 400,000 tpy of CO₂ and integrate renewable power, green hydrogen, carbon capture and fuel production into a carbon-recycling system.

Dongde describes it as China’s first and largest SAF demonstration project of its type. It is intended to expand SAF production in northwest China while helping traditional chemical industries transition toward lower-carbon, higher-value products.

TOP STORY

FEATURE: Canada’s new nature taskforce begins shaping foundation of country’s nature market

Canada’s nature finance taskforce will look to set the foundation for how conservation and ecosystem markets advance in the country, starting with defining who should be involved and how they can contribute.

Nature-related shareholder resolutions persisted through US regulatory upheaval in the 2026 proxy season, as investor attention shifted towards regenerative agriculture, according to Carbon Pulse analysis.

A coalition of legal experts and environmental groups from across Latin America launched a template of a law in Mexico City on Thursday to support legislators in criminalising the most severe forms of environmental harm and destruction.

EMEA

EU nature credits – The European Commission’s expert group on nature credits is holding its fourth meeting over Oct.1-2. The gathering aims to advance the EU’s ongoing work to design the overarching frameworks for a bloc-wide nature credit market by the end of next year. The meeting comes as the European Commission is set to present its plans at the COP17 UN biodiversity summit in Yerevan, Armenia, next month.

ASIA PACIFIC

World Congress on Snakes – The Sri Lankan city of Kandy is hosting the first World Congress on Snakes from Oct. 1-4 covering conservation, snake biology, and public health. More than 400 delegates from 25 countries are expected to attend the conference, reported Mongabay. The event will be held under 12 themes ranging from snake biology to policies for human coexistence with snakes. These include safeguarding snakes and their habitats under global pressure, and the management of captive snakes for conservation.

Target doubled – The Asian Infrastructure Investment Bank (AIIB) will aim to double its annual financing to $20 bln by 2030, prioritising infrastructure for climate resilience, renewable energy, and nature conservation, alongside other focus areas like digital transformation and regional connectivity. This was announced by AIIB President Jiayi Zou at the development bank’s 11th annual meeting in Qatar this week, marking the start of its second decade of operation. AIIB has said that it is devoting more attention to integrating biodiversity and nature-based solutions into its infrastructure investment considerations.

Biochar potential – Japanese developer Asian Gateway’s proposal to launch a feasibility study for rice husk-based biochar production in Cambodia’s Battambang province has been selected for government grants. The study aims to verify the commercial viability of an entire value chain, from converting rice husks into biochar and applying it to farmland to conducting MRV and generating credits under the Joint Crediting Mechanism. It will also consider an integrated approach that applies both the alternate wetting and drying method and rice-husk derived biochar to the same fields.

AMERICAS

Deep sea – Conservation groups filed a lawsuit on Wednesday challenging the US National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration’s certification of a seabed mineral exploration application. The lawsuit, from Conservation Council for Hawaiʻi and the Center for Biological Diversity, represented by Earthjustice, alleged that the authority had breached requirements on transparency and public participation. The application from the Metals Company USA was the first to receive certification for deep-sea mining exploration since President Trump took office, while several other applications are pending, according to the centre.

Another US mining dispute – The Centre for Biological Diversity and Patagonia Area Resource Alliance have sued the Trump administration in the US District Court for the District of Arizona over its decision to approve the expansion of South32’s Hermosa mine onto federal public lands in southern Arizona. The lawsuit challenges approvals by the US Forest Service and US Fish and Wildlife Service that would expand industrial mining across more than 21,000 hectares of public land in the Coronado National Forest. The mine is located in the Patagonia Mountains of Arizona, one of the state’s most biodiverse and ecologically significant mountain ranges.

Species recovery – Two US senators have presented draft legislation to change the implementation of the US Endangered Species Act’s species recovery efforts. The proposals aim to standardise conservation efforts, encourage conservation efforts by private landowners, and help endangered species to recover, said senators Adam Schiff and Pete Ricketts. The bipartisan bill comes amid a wider debate over the future of the Endangered Species Act, including lawsuits by 21 states challenging recent Trump administration changes to existing species protections.

Georgia SAF coalition – A group of Georgia businesses, forestry, and agriculture producers have teamed up to create the Georgia Sustainable Aviation Fuel (SAF) Coalition, a new partnership focused on positioning the state as a US leader in sustainable aviation fuel research and production. The coalition aims to accelerate the growth of agri- and forestry-derived SAF by coordinating public-private partnerships, better aligning university research with industry needs, and considering new avenues to attract investment. The coalition is aiming to build upon momentum created by the Keep Georgia Forested Act, legislation that encourages investment into forestry manufacturing, including the production of biofuels from Georgia-based feedstocks.

Wetland restoration – Energy company Orsted announced this week it has started construction of its Blackwater Solar project in New Mexico, alongside a $100,000 investment in local wetland conservation. The funding will support restoration of a site near Melrose, through a partnership with Playa Lakes Joint Venture. The initiative will focus on restoring bird habitat and improving the biological function of the wetland.

INTERNATIONAL

Current affairs – Marine technology company Blue Carbon International (BCI) and environmental finance advisory AeonLoop announced a partnership via LinkedIn this week to help governments measure the value of marine ecosystems and develop financial structures to attract institutional investment. The companies said they would combine BCI’s marine science and natural-capital accounting capabilities with AeonLoop’s expertise in financial structuring, Article 6 programme design, and access to capital markets. The partnership targets new sovereign opportunities beyond BCI’s existing work in the Bahamas, with the companies potentially jointly marketing their services and involving one another in new engagements.

title: Business, Forestry and Agriculture Leaders Unite to Advance Sustainable Aviation Fuels
description:

text:
Georgia agriculture and forestry producers and the business community have teamed up to create the Georgia Sustainable Aviation Fuel (SAF) Coalition, a new partnership focused on positioning the state as a national leader in sustainable aviation fuel research and production. Founding organizations include the Metro Atlanta Chamber, Georgia Farm Bureau, Georgia Forestry Association, and Delta Air Lines, working together to accelerate domestic production of biofuels that utilize Georgia grown agriculture and forestry feedstocks.

Sustainable aviation fuel can be produced from a variety of feedstocks to reduce emissions from air transportation and is designed to be compatible with existing aircraft and fueling infrastructure. While SAF currently represents a small share of global fuel supply, demand is rising quickly across global markets as production scales and interest from airlines and customers continues to accelerate.

Thanks to strong political and business leadership, Georgia has built a foundation to grow the capacity needed to produce ag- and forestry-derived SAF. The Georgia SAF Coalition aims to accelerate that growth by better coordinating public-private partnerships, more closely aligning university research with industry needs, and considering avenues to attract investment.

The coalition’s launch builds on the momentum of Georgia’s Keep Georgia Forested Act, which encourages investment in forestry manufacturing, including the production of biofuels from Georgia-based feedstocks. The legislation, signed into law by Gov. Brian Kemp in May 2026, enhances Georgia’s competitiveness by allowing certain tax credits to be transferred. This change allows companies to monetize credits during the critical early stages of construction and operations, when workers are being hired and capital needs are highest. That investment reaches beyond aviation, creating new markets for Georgia farmers and forest landowners and sustaining demand for locally grown feedstocks.

Georgia’s combination of agriculture and forestry resources, world-class research institutions, logistics infrastructure, and industry leadership positions the state to become a leader in sustainable aviation fuel development and production.

“This is about aligning Georgia’s natural strengths with real market demand,” said Katie Kirkpatrick, President and CEO of the Metro Atlanta Chamber. “Georgia is making a serious play for a piece of the emerging sustainable aviation fuel market. By bringing global companies, producers, researchers, and the agricultural community all to the same table, we are building a powerful biofuels ecosystem that serves the entire state and connects us to the world.”

“For farmers across Georgia, sustainable aviation fuel could open new markets for our agricultural commodities, offering new opportunities and increased profitability,” said Tom McCall, President of Georgia Farm Bureau. “Partnerships like the Georgia SAF Coalition help connect broader economic innovation to agriculture, the number one industry in our state.”

“Georgia is the number one forestry state in the nation, and our state’s 22 million acres of working forests are among the most productive in the world,” said Tim Lowrimore, President & CEO, Georgia Forestry Association. “SAF provides a chance to put that resource to work in a growing market which means new demand for landowners, new jobs in rural Georgia and new manufacturing investment in the communities that need it most. This coalition makes sure producers are at the table from day one.”

“Georgia is well positioned to become a national leader in SAF,” said Peter Carter, President of Delta Air Lines. “The Georgia SAF Coalition unites organizations committed to advancing that opportunity. Together, we can power the growth of a SAF industry that strengthens Georgia’s economy, supports innovation, and creates lasting benefits for communities across the state.”

“Sustainable aviation fuel represents a significant opportunity for the nation’s agricultural and forestry sectors and the rural communities that support them. The Georgia SAF Coalition brings together producers, industry leaders and other stakeholders to help unlock new markets, drive innovation and strengthen American energy leadership. Georgia has the resources and expertise to play an important role in the future of SAF while creating economic opportunities across the state. I am glad to see the public-private partnerships behind the effort to allow Sustainable Aviation Fuel to take flight,” said Stephen Vaden, Deputy Secretary, U.S. Department of Agriculture

Prior to launch, coalition members joined the Georgia Research Alliance in successfully advocating for state funding for a Georgia Research Alliance Eminent Scholar. This research will focus on the forestry sector and help identify emerging opportunities, including biofuels.

Founding members of the Georgia SAF Coalition include Delta Air Lines, Georgia Farm Bureau, Georgia Forestry Association, and the Metro Atlanta Chamber. Anchor partners include Boeing, Cox Enterprises, and Norfolk Southern, with additional support from supporting partners RYAM and Gulfstream Aerospace.

Research, education and community partners include the Georgia Institute of Technology, Georgia Research Alliance, Georgia Southern University, Technical College System of Georgia, University of Georgia, Clean Cities Georgia, Georgia Agribusiness Council, Georgia Association of Manufacturers, Hartsfield-Jackson Atlanta International Airport, and the National Federation of Independent Business.

The coalition immediate priorities are: recruiting SAF and biofuels facilities to Georgia, connecting university research to industry needs, and building the supply chain that links Georgia's forests and farms to aviation customers.

text:
What's the deal? Northern Ireland cleantech company CATAGEN has secured government-backed commercial finance to launch a new division focused on sustainable aviation fuel (SAF) technology. The debt financing is backed by a guarantee from UK Export Finance (UKEF), the UK government's export credit agency.

What's the endgame? The Belfast company builds technology aimed at cutting carbon and other emissions. Its Green Flight unit produces small modular units that make SAF with very low carbon emissions and can be deployed across sites and expanded as demand grows.

Why now? The money helps CATAGEN move from late-stage development into commercial production. It also strengthens the company's intellectual property position and international growth plans, chief executive and founder Dr Andrew Woods said.

UKEF says the backing should help CATAGEN reach more overseas customers. The announcement came ahead of UKEF's Northern Ireland Business Forum in Belfast on October 6, where exporters and officials were due to discuss support for international trade.

What else? Alongside the SAF push, CATAGEN continues to expand its Green Emissions Testing business, which helps vehicle manufacturers and industrial customers meet emissions standards in global markets. Its partners include ROUSH, Ducati, Ryanair, Shell Aviation Ireland, Vinci Airports, and Loganair.

The signal: The financing fits the UK government's industrial strategy, which puts clean growth and sustainable aviation at the centre of its manufacturing and export ambitions. For Northern Ireland, it reinforces the region's role in low-carbon aviation and clean technology, with ministers citing support for skilled local jobs.

title: Small Refineries, Big Consequences: What Exemptions Mean for Biofuel Demand
description:
By Scott Gerlt, PhD • ASA Chief Economist Small refinery exemptions can undercut headline biofuel blending numbers with much of the burden falling on biomass-based diesel.
The exemptions cost 4 billion gallons of biofuel demand.
In our example, EPA would divide the 20 billion gallons of intended biofuel use across the 160 billion gallons of remaining obligated fuel.

Small refinery exemptions have been controversial for many years as they historically gutted the biofuel blending.
text:
By Scott Gerlt, PhD • ASA Chief Economist

Small refinery exemptions can undercut headline biofuel blending numbers with much of the burden falling on biomass-based diesel.

Since the enactment of the Renewable Fuel Standard in 2005, no single issue deriving from the law generates as much controversy as Small Refinery Exemptions. SREs continue to be litigated and debated 20 years later and have even led to recent attempts to revise the RFS to deal with the issue. Although not well understood outside biofuel circles, SREs heavily affect biofuel demand and subsequently agricultural prices. EPA’s current methods for dealing with the issue have largely removed their negative effects from agriculture, but there is no guarantee this treatment will continue in the future.

History

Under the RFS, petroleum refineries and importers are obligated parties that must demonstrate that biofuels have been blended into petroleum fuels at the percents prescribed by EPA. Each gallon of biofuel produced or imported is associated with Renewable Identification Numbers. When the biofuel is blended with petroleum, the RINs can be detached from the biofuel and turned into EPA to show the proper amount of biofuel was blended. Alternatively, an obligated party can make up a shortfall in its own blending by purchasing RINs from other parties that have excess.

The RFS intended to ease small refineries (defined as processing less than 75,000 barrels per day) into compliance with the program by exempting all small refineries from RFS compliance from 2006 until 2011[1]. Beginning in 2011, individual refineries could petition EPA for an extension by demonstrating that RFS compliance would cause “disproportionate economic hardship.”

A detailed history of SREs would fill a dissertation, but Figure 1 shows the historical exemption levels compared to the overall biofuel blending mandate. An easy way to think of this is the percent of the mandate waived through SREs. SREs peaked in 2017 at over 9% of the blending obligation after relatively low levels in the previous years. Starting in 2020, SREs were generally between four and five percent of obligations before shooting up to the second highest level in recent history in 2025.

Figure 1

SREs Explained

Understanding how SREs impact biofuel demand can best be demonstrated by a simple example with manufactured numbers. Suppose gasoline and diesel on-road consumption for the U.S. totals 200 billion gallons per year. Also suppose that EPA wants 20 billion gallons of biofuels blended into the fuel supply. In this case, they would set the blending rate at 10%.

Now suppose that after the EPA sets the blend rate at 10% that they exempt refineries responsible for 40 billion gallons of fuel from compliance. This would reduce the total volume of the obligated parties to 160 billion gallons. As a result, only 16 billion gallons of biofuels would be consumed. The exemptions cost 4 billion gallons of biofuel demand.

EPA does have one tool available to them to address this situation. They can increase the blending rate on the remaining obligated parties to make up for the exemptions. This is called reallocation. In our example, EPA would divide the 20 billion gallons of intended biofuel use across the 160 billion gallons of remaining obligated fuel. The exempted parties would blend no biofuel while the remaining parties would blend at a rate of 12.5%. The total biofuel consumption would remain at 20 billion gallons, but some parties now blend nothing and others blend more. If exemptions are granted, this option allows for biofuels to avoid negative impacts.

While this simple example demonstrates the overall impact on biofuels, it excludes some important nuances of the RFS. There are multiple blending rate targets in the RFS that each have their own biofuel eligibility. In essence, there isn’t one “biofuel” but many with differing rules about which blending rates they can help fill. This detail leaves biomass-based diesel (biodiesel, renewable diesel and sustainable aviation fuel) uniquely exposed to SREs.

Understanding this issue involves a brief explanation of the biofuel categories in the RFS. For simplicity, this explanation will omit cellulosic biofuels, which are a very small part of the program. The remaining categories are:

Biomass-based diesel (D4): Biodiesel, renewable diesel and sustainable aviation fuel that has at least a 50% reduction in greenhouse gas emissions.

Advanced biofuels (D5): Non-biomass-based diesel biofuels with at least a 50% GHG reduction.

Conventional (D6): Biofuels with a GHG reduction between 20% and 50%. Note that the RFS specifies that this is the only category that corn ethanol may participate in.

EPA sets targets and corresponding blending levels for each of these categories. For the categories listed, fuels with a lower number D code may be used for the blending targets corresponding to higher number D codes. For example, biomass-based diesel (D4) RINs can be used for advanced (D5) or conventional (D6) blending requirements. The opposite is not true, and D6 RINs cannot be used for any other obligations.

The economics of the program design require that biofuels generating higher number D codes must be cheaper to produce than those with lower D codes. Otherwise, biomass-based diesel would simply replace ethanol production in the conventional category. In effect, there is no ethanol mandate in the RFS but only a category it can fill at a lower cost up to blending limits.

Figure 1 shows how this works in practice. EPA set the conventional (D6) target at 15 billion RINs for 2026. However, the agency only expects ethanol to fill 14.27 billion RINs[2] of this. The rest is backfilled by BBD. The advanced category is similar with BBD filling 380 million RINs. When an SRE is granted, each of the categories (D codes) is proportionally reduced with the biofuel on top of the stack taking the loss of demand hit first. In other words, the bar shrinks pushing out what was on top of the stack. As a result, BBD doesn’t just lose what is in the D4 category but loses across all three categories until it is pushed out. For this reason, BBD generally takes the bulk of SRE losses. Empirical analysis supports this conclusion.

Figure 2

Set 2 Changed SRE Treatment

EPA sought to proactively address the SRE issue in the RVOs for 2026 and 2027 that were released in March 2026. When the blending levels were released, there were over 180 outstanding SRE petitions that could exempt about 12 billion RINs. RINs must be used in the year of generation or the following year, and EPA expected almost no outstanding RIN obligations for pre-2024 compliance years. EPA made decisions on 2023 and 2024 SREs but did not yet know the final level for 2025. Instead, for 2025 EPA used a three-year average for exempted gallons to estimate the expected SREs. The agency then reallocated 70% of the RINs provided by SREs onto the volume obligations for 2026 and 2027.

Table 1: EPA Estimated Exempted RINs from SREs in Set 2

EPA assumed that 7.55 billion gallons of gasoline and diesel would be exempted in 2025 with SREs. EPA carried that assumption of exempted gallons forward for 2026 and 2027. Given the percentage standards before reallocation, this results in 1,121 RINs in 2026 and 1,141 RINs in 2027. EPA fully reallocated these amounts into the RVO for 2026 and 2027. The agency stated they intend to proactively reallocate all SREs in future set rules but did not intend to reopen Set 2 to address any differences between their assumed SRE levels and actual SRE levels.

The stated intention to not recalculate the percentage standards in the middle of the set rule provided assurance to markets that they could proceed without worrying about changes midstream. However, it did not account for other factors that did change midstream. These factors include “more small refineries requesting exemptions and changes in financial circumstances.”

Table 2 shows the actual granting of SREs. Calendar year 2024 ended up almost 200 million RINs above expected levels. The big change was in 2025 where almost 800 million more RINs were granted in SREs than initially estimated. Instead of 7.55 billion gallons of exempted fuel, 13.40 billion gallons were exempted. The volume of exempted RINs will likely further increase in 2026 and 2027 above what was planned for due to higher percent obligations on those years (Table 2).

Table 2: Actual Exempted RINs from SREs

EPA has committed to reallocating 100% of the additional 2025 SRE RINs above the originally estimated 990 million through a supplemental rule to Set 2. If EPA keeps the same formulas originally used in Set 2, the reallocated RINs will increase the percent standards for 2027 while 2026 standards remain unchanged. However, the likely higher SRE volumes for compliance years 2026 and 2027 will likely also need to be addressed, either in a supplemental rule or Set 3.

Not only do SREs cause market disruption, but rumors of SREs can as well. Before news broke on August 20th that the administration was considering granting more SREs, the D6 RIN was $2.25 according to Argus. Within a week, it dropped to $1.78 and has now sits at about $2.00. The simple uncertainty over a period of slightly more than a week wiped out value for biofuel producers and subsequently farmers.

EPA’s plan to proactively reallocate 100% of SREs gives as much certainty as possible if SREs are to be granted. While granting more SREs for 2025 than expected has caused disruption, the declaration of intent to reallocate all of the additional exempted volumes calmed markets. Continuation of this calm is dependent on quickly moving through a supplemental rulemaking process to incorporate the reallocation into the percent standards. While the SREs are finalized, the reallocation is not. EPA will also need to consider how to handle likely increased SREs for 2026 and 2027 as well.

Small refinery exemptions have been controversial for many years as they historically gutted the biofuel blending. Even 20 years after the RFS was passed, the transitory mechanism still causes volatility and uncertainty in biofuel markets. While headline RVO numbers often receive much press, without knowing actual SREs and their treatment the RVO numbers by themselves merely reflect a starting point.

[1]For 2011 and 2012, 14 small refineries were granted an extension of the initial exemption for the year. Another 10 that did not receive an automatic extension were granted exemptions based on petitions for 2011. That number changed to 9 in 2012.

title: Jordan's water plan risks locking in demand for Israeli gas
description:
“We have carried out environmental impact studies for the Aqaba desalination plant,” the spokesperson added.
“Every Jordanian living in a village or city … can feel, especially in the summer, that the amount of water reaching their home is not enough,” said University of Jordan water science professor Elias Salameh.

In the meantime, Jordan’s National Electric Power Company (NEPCO) remains heavily dependent on Israeli gas for electricity generation, industry experts say.

text:
On the desert shores of the Red Sea, Jordan plans to build a vast desalination plant to send drinking water hundreds of kilometres across its arid interior to the capital, Amman - bolstering climate resilience and reducing reliance on Israel for the vital resource.

As climate change exacerbates water scarcity in Jordan, a deterioration in the country’s already prickly ties with Israel since the start of the Gaza war has underscored the strategic importance of the roughly $6-billion desalination initiative, billed by its backers as a strategic climate adaptation project.

But despite receiving $295 million in support for the project from the UN’s Green Climate Fund (GCF), the energy-hungry plant - which will double the power needs of Jordan’s water sector - will get no more than 27% of its electricity from a purpose-built solar farm in the desert near the plant in Aqaba. The rest will come from the grid, whose power is mostly generated by fossil gas.

To get salt out of sea water, it has to be pushed at high pressure through a membrane - a process requiring huge amounts of electricity.

The annual planet-heating emissions from producing the non-renewable power needed for the plant would be equivalent to having 160,000 petrol-run cars on the road for a year, according to an analysis by Climate Home News of figures provided by the project’s developers to the GCF - the world's largest multilateral fund to help developing countries tackle climate change.

Such forecasts prompted a warning from its independent technical advisory panel and criticism by climate campaigners, but the GCF board nevertheless approved the financing at a meeting late last year, with GCF Executive Director Mafalda Duarte hailing it as a “milestone project”.

A GCF spokesperson told Climate Home News its design “required the balanced optimisation of multiple objectives”, among them water security, financing considerations and climate-related benefits.

Asked to respond to concerns about the project’s sustainability, a spokesperson for Jordan’s Ministry of Water and Irrigation said the plant is key to tackling the nation’s water deficit, in tandem with other steps to conserve supplies such as managing leaks.

“We have carried out environmental impact studies for the Aqaba desalination plant,” the spokesperson added. “All donor countries reviewed and approved these studies.”

Dry and getting drier

Jordan is already one of the world’s most water-stressed countries, and climate change impacts mean the country of about 11 million people is getting less rain at a time of population growth, in part due to the arrival of refugees from the war in Syria.

Half of Jordanian homes currently receive water for less than 24 hours a week and many pay to get tanker trucks to deliver extra water despite the high cost.

“Every Jordanian living in a village or city … can feel, especially in the summer, that the amount of water reaching their home is not enough,” said University of Jordan water science professor Elias Salameh.

At the same time, heightened political tensions in the region are raising fears over a long-standing water supply accord with Israel.

Prominent Israeli news outlet Ynet quoted government officials as saying last year that - until Jordan ends its criticism of Israel’s actions in Gaza - it would no longer send Jordan 100 million cubic metres of water a year, as it has been doing since 2021.

Instead, media reports said Israel had decided to send just the 50 million cubic metres required by the 1994 Israel-Jordan peace agreement.

That makes the desalination project all the more urgent, Motasem Saidan, a former water minister who pushed it forward, told Climate Home News.

"Relying on neighbouring countries for sources of the most important resource for life is risky. You need to have self-sufficiency and water security,” Saidan added.

Largest single GCF investment

French multinationals Meridiam and Suez have been awarded the contract to lead construction of the desalination facility, which Suez says will be one of the largest of its kind globally.

Scheduled for completion in 2030, it will turn 300 million cubic metres of seawater a year - enough to fill 120,000 Olympic-sized swimming pools - into drinking water, which will then be carried by pipeline more than 400 km across the desert to reservoirs near Amman, home to nearly half of Jordan’s population.

The GCF will support it with a $220 million loan and a $75 million grant. While that represents a small share of the total cost, Duarte said last year it represented “the largest single investment in one project that we have made”.

But the GCF’s decision to pour millions into the project followed strong criticism from climate campaigners, initial opposition from some of the fund’s board members and a warning by its independent technical advisory panel (ITAP) over its potential impact on emissions.

The emissions it aims to avoid rest on the timely completion of a 65-km transmission line connecting the desalination plant to the solar farm. Without this, the plant will run entirely on Jordan’s gas-dominated grid, the ITAP said in its assessment report.

Moreover, while the government plans to make the power supplied by the national grid greener in the years ahead, there is no guarantee this will be achieved, the report added.

Such issues make the project “difficult to reconcile with climate finance objectives”, the ITAP said, adding there is a significant risk that “concessional resources could end up subsidising a high-carbon, high-cost water pathway”.

Still, the ITAP concluded that “given the dire water situation in Jordan”, the project's benefits outweighed those concerns and recommended approval to the board.

Bigger renewables role deemed unfeasible

The possibility of producing more of the plant’s electricity from solar power and batteries was dismissed by the project’s proposer and co-funder - the World Bank’s International Finance Corporation (IFC) - and the GCF as too expensive and impractical, a decision critics see as a wasted opportunity to shift to clean energy.

The companies that carried out the project’s environmental and social impact assessment - Eco Consult and Energies Group - said the option of sourcing all power from renewables “was not studied in detail” because it was seen as unfeasible.

Asked to comment, the GCF spokesperson said the fund supported that conclusion, citing renewable energy’s intermittency and noting that excess solar power produced would be wasted because there is no provision for it to be sold to the grid.

“The optimum design of such a critical life-line desalination project for Jordan is fundamentally a whole-of-system water optimisation challenge rather than a standalone energy storage exercise,” the spokesperson said.

Instead, the plan’s advocates have touted potential emissions reductions as the pipeline replaces water trucks. They say the solar farm set to supply more than a quarter of the desalination plant’s power will prevent 6.7 million tonnes of CO2-equivalent being emitted over its 26-year projected lifetime.

Saidan, the former water minister, said the urgency of providing water must take priority over gas dependency concerns.

“This is not the time to raise such issues,” he told Climate Home News.

But Kostanta Rangelova, a global electricity analyst at think-tank Ember, said the plant could “easily” get at least 80% of its power from solar with batteries, pointing to Jordan’s abundant sunshine and the plunging costs of the equipment needed.

Such systems are set to power large facilities elsewhere in the region, like a luxury Red Sea resort just over the Saudi border and a data centre near Abu Dhabi, she said. Jordan’s own energy sector strategy, published in May, lists increasing battery storage as a strategic target.

Rangelova noted that with battery prices falling significantly in recent years, the cost of solar plus battery storage is now competitive with grid power in many places, particularly in countries like Jordan that have a lot of sun but currently rely on expensive imported gas.

“With solar and batteries, Jordan (could) use homegrown electricity not just during daytime hours, but round-the-clock, which can significantly strengthen its energy security position,” she added.

Lesser of two evils

Using more renewables in the project could also help reduce demand for Israeli natural gas imports - a sensitive issue in Jordan.

“[The desalination plant] will not be viable if we depend on gas supplied by the Israeli occupation,” Mahmoud Amin Al-Hayari, an activist with the General Trade Union of Electricity Workers in Jordan, told Climate Home News.

Jordan’s government is working to develop new sources of gas imports to diversify its current supply, and also wants to boost domestic gas production, alongside renewables.

In the meantime, Jordan’s National Electric Power Company (NEPCO) remains heavily dependent on Israeli gas for electricity generation, industry experts say. Latest government figures from 2024 show the country got 58% of its electric power from gas.

Most of that gas is likely to be Israeli. “About 57% of the electricity that NEPCO supplies to distribution companies comes from gas imported from Israel,” a Jordanian energy and conflict analyst told Climate Home News, asking to speak anonymously due to the sensitivity of the subject.

The spokesperson for Jordan’s Ministry of Water and Irrigation declined to comment on the source of the gas that would help power the Aqaba desalination project.

The issue has gained attention due to several security-related gas supply disruptions from Israel related to the conflict in the Middle East.

For countries like Jordan, a net fuel importer, the energy security case for boosting renewables is a no-brainer, said Ember’s Rangelova. “Unlike imported fossil fuels, the sun cannot be turned off,” she said.

text:
Brazil’s state-controlled energy company Petrobras is developing two Cardano-based projects to monitor data on environmentally friendly aviation fuel and renewable diesel.

Petrobras, one of Brazil’s largest companies, has begun using the Cardano blockchain to verify environmental data related to low-carbon fuels. The initiative, announced by the Cardano Foundation, encompasses two research and development projects: one for sustainable aviation fuel and another for Diesel R, which is produced using partially renewable raw materials.

The aviation project aims to prevent multiple companies from claiming ownership of the emission reduction rights resulting from the use of sustainable fuel. In this model, known as “book-and-claim,” an airline can purchase the environmental benefit even if the fuel is physically used on another flight. Therefore, the original owner of the right, the party to whom it is transferred, and when it was used must be reliably recorded.

Developed by Petrobras, the system represents each sustainable aviation fuel characteristic with a standardized token on Cardano. Tokens can be created, transferred, and permanently retired once the environmental benefit has been used up. This aims to prevent the same emission reduction from being claimed a second time.

Passengers can also enter their departure and arrival airports into the system to calculate the environmental benefit associated with their flight. They can then receive a verifiable document linked to a source fuel certificate.

The second project focuses on Diesel R, a product containing renewable raw materials such as vegetable or animal fats. The plan is to record data on Cardano throughout the fuel’s production, transportation, and usage phases. This data can help companies report indirect emissions from their suppliers and customers.

Both studies are still in the research phase. Neither Petrobras nor the Cardano Foundation has announced a date for large-scale commercial use of the systems. The amount of fuel being monitored and whether the projects will have a direct impact on ADA usage have also not yet been specified.

text:
Northern Ireland cleantech company CATAGEN has secured government-backed commercial finance to launch a new business division focused on technology for sustainable aviation fuel. The funding supports the Belfast group's push from late-stage development into commercial production as demand grows for lower-carbon aviation solutions.

Funding supports commercial scale-up

As reported by GOV.UK, the financing is backed by a guarantee from UK Export Finance, the UK government's export credit agency, and is intended to help CATAGEN build on the progress of its subsidiary ClimaHtech Green Flight. The Titanic Quarter-based company develops technology aimed at cutting carbon and other emissions, with its Green Flight unit producing systems linked to sustainable aviation fuel, or SAF.

CATAGEN says its Green Flight technology helps produce SAF with very low carbon emissions through small modular production units that can be deployed across different locations and expanded as demand increases. Chief executive and founder Dr Andrew Woods says the support helps bridge the gap between late-stage product development and commercialisation, while also strengthening the company's intellectual property position and international growth plans.

Alongside the SAF push, the company continues to expand CATAGEN Green Emissions Testing, a business that provides testing services to help vehicle manufacturers and other industrial customers meet strict emissions standards in global markets.

Regional export and industrial strategy impact

The announcement fits with the UK government's industrial strategy, which places clean growth and sustainable aviation at the centre of manufacturing and export ambitions. Ministers say the financing supports skilled jobs in Northern Ireland and reinforces the region's role in low-carbon aviation and clean technology.

CATAGEN was founded by Dr Woods, who holds a PhD in mechanical engineering from Queen's University Belfast, and works with a broader supply chain across Northern Ireland and the UK. Its partners include ROUSH, Zenvo, Ducati, Ryanair, Shell Aviation Ireland, Vinci Airports and LoganAir, reflecting the company's reach across Europe and the U.S.

UK Export Finance says the backing should help the company move into commercial production and reach more overseas customers. The announcement comes ahead of UKEF's Northern Ireland Business Forum in Belfast on 6 October, where exporters, finance specialists and government officials are due to discuss support for businesses trading internationally.

text:
The coalition aims to advance SAF production and drive economic investment across Georgia. SAF is an alternative jet fuel made from renewable feedstocks that can significantly reduce lifecycle carbon emissions compared to conventional jet fuel.

During an event at the Delta Flight Museum, elected officials, industry leaders and coalition partners gathered to highlight Georgia's opportunity to become a leader in sustainable aviation fuel production. Speakers included Georgia House Speaker Jon Burns, Georgia Agriculture Commissioner Tyler Harper, Metro Atlanta Chamber President and CEO Katie Kirkpatrick and Delta President Peter Carter.

"Georgia is well positioned to become a national leader in SAF," said Peter Carter, President of Delta Air Lines. "The Georgia SAF Coalition unites organizations committed to advancing that opportunity. Together, we can power the growth of a SAF industry that strengthens Georgia’s economy, supports innovation and creates lasting benefits for communities across the state.”

The coalition builds on momentum created by this year's Keep Georgia Forested Act, legislation that encourages investment in forestry manufacturing and creates new opportunities to convert Georgia-grown agricultural and forestry feedstocks into products such as sustainable aviation fuel.

Priorities include strengthening public-private partnerships, supporting research and commercialization, attracting investment, advancing policies that support industry growth and connecting Georgia's existing strengths to emerging opportunities.

As home to Delta's global headquarters and the world's busiest airport, Georgia is already helping shape the future of aviation. Combined with the nation's largest forestry resource base, strong agricultural production, leading research institutions and a robust logistics network, the state is uniquely positioned to build a sustainable aviation fuel ecosystem that supports farmers, foresters and local communities while creating new economic opportunities across Georgia.

SAF is widely viewed as one of the most promising tools available today to reduce lifecycle carbon emissions from air travel, and Georgia has the feedstock resources, research capabilities and business leadership needed to help scale the industry.

title: Cardano Foundation pushes renewable fuel traceability forward with blockchain
description:
As part of an ongoing R&D collaboration, the teams have delivered two blockchain applications focused on sustainable aviation fuel (SAF) and Diesel R, Petrobras’ brand of renewable fuel.
These initiatives address different parts of the renewable fuel lifecycle.
Making sustainable aviation fuel claims traceable The SAF R&D project brings together Petrobras, PUC-Rio through its blockchain center Ledger Labs, and the Cardano Foundation.
Extending traceability across renewable diesel A second Petrobras project, developed with PUC-Rio, applies Cardano to Diesel R, Petrobras’ brand of renewable diesel.
“The energy transition will depend as much on trust as it does on new fuels,” said Rafael Fraga, LATAM Business Development Lead at the Cardano Foundation.
text:
The Cardano Foundation, the independent, Swiss-based not-for-profit organization dedicated to advancing Cardano as public digital infrastructure, on Sept. 30 announced two new initiatives with Petrobras, Brazil’s state-controlled energy firm and one of Latin America’s most valuable companies. As part of an ongoing R&D collaboration, the teams have delivered two blockchain applications focused on sustainable aviation fuel (SAF) and Diesel R, Petrobras’ brand of renewable fuel.

Brazil’s oil and gas market is projected to reach USD 28.82 billion by 2031, underscoring the scale of the sector in which these initiatives are being developed. Against that backdrop, both projects focus on a specific challenge: making environmental claims and fuel lifecycle data easier to trace and verify.

These initiatives address different parts of the renewable fuel lifecycle. For SAF, Cardano connects a physical fuel certificate to a digital record of the associated environmental gains, creating a clear trail from the original certificate through to the final claim. For renewable diesel, the technology links information across production, transportation and use, improving visibility over the fuel journey and the emissions-related data associated with it.

Making sustainable aviation fuel claims traceable

The SAF R&D project brings together Petrobras, PUC-Rio through its blockchain center Ledger Labs, and the Cardano Foundation. Sustainable aviation fuel is a lower-carbon alternative to conventional jet fuel that can be used within existing aviation infrastructure. As adoption grows, airlines and passengers also need credible ways to verify the environmental benefit associated with its use.

The project uses a Book-and-Claim model, which separates that environmental benefit from the physical fuel itself. This allows the benefit to be assigned to an airline, company or passenger even when the SAF is produced or used elsewhere. Cardano provides the traceable record behind the process, showing where the benefit originated, who it was assigned to and that it has only been claimed once.

The application also extends to individual passengers. Travelers can enter their departure and destination airports, calculate the corresponding CS-SAF amount – the digital token used to represent the SAF environmental benefit – and receive a certificate recording their route, distance traveled and allocation. This links the passenger’s claim back to the original SAF certificate.

Extending traceability across renewable diesel

A second Petrobras project, developed with PUC-Rio, applies Cardano to Diesel R, Petrobras’ brand of renewable diesel. The proposed model creates digital checkpoints across production, transportation and use, converting information from each stage into a continuous record of the fuel’s lifecycle.

This is particularly relevant for reporting of Scope 3 greenhouse-gas emissions, which covers indirect emissions generated across a company’s wider value chain and often relies on data spread across suppliers, logistics providers and other external systems. By connecting those record the model can create a clearer supply-chain history and strengthen the traceability and auditability of information used in emissions accounting.

“The energy transition will depend as much on trust as it does on new fuels,” said Rafael Fraga, LATAM Business Development Lead at the Cardano Foundation. “As value chains become more complex, proving where environmental data comes from, how it moves and who can rely on it becomes critical. Public blockchain gives us the opportunity to make that trust part of the system by design, providing industries with a shared, verifiable foundation for the next generation of energy markets.”

The two projects apply the same underlying principle to different parts of the energy transition: creating a reliable digital trail for information that today often sits across fragmented systems, organizations and supply chains.

The work adds to the Cardano Foundation’s growing portfolio of real-world blockchain applications in Brazil, demonstrating how public digital infrastructure can support industries where provenance, transparency and auditability are increasingly important.

text:
From Canadian crude to customers around the world, Phillips 66’s Central Corridor works in symphony to keep energy moving

A barrel of oil to our refineries rarely follows a straight line. It may start with a purchase in Western Canada, move through pipelines and storage, be processed at a refinery and reach customers as gasoline, diesel or jet fuel. Or, when market conditions point elsewhere, it may move to the Gulf Coast for export on a vessel.

That’s integration in motion, connecting commercial decisions, physical assets and customer demand across one value chain.

This Today & Tomorrow spotlight shows how operations in Phillips 66’s Central Corridor work together, creating a distinctive advantage that drives value.

Right barrel, right market

Phillips 66’s Calgary, Alberta, office is key to the Central Corridor.

Reliable source of supply

The team manages crude supply, trading, scheduling and logistics, connecting the system to Western Canadian crude, a reliable and important source of supply for Phillips 66 refineries and global markets.

Teams weigh market conditions, refinery needs, transportation options and product demand to determine where each barrel delivers the most value.

This requires close coordination across teams, locations and regions. Together, they move crude by pipeline, rail, ship or truck — getting the right barrel to the right market at the right time.

The Calgary office is more than just crude

Learn more from Chris Breen, crude trading lead, Americas and Calgary office lead, in the video below.

From supply to customers

From Montana’s Big Sky Country to the Texas Panhandle, Phillips 66’s Central Corridor is a network built around a simple idea: Connect the right assets to the products people need.

Built to work together

Four refineries — Billings in Montana, Borger in Texas, Ponca City in Oklahoma and Wood River in Illinois — turn crude oil into the fuels and products that keep communities, businesses and economies moving.

The advantage is not just the scale of those refineries, but how they work together. Their interconnectivity gives Phillips 66 greater flexibility to move crude and refined products across the system, respond to changing supply and demand, and serve customers across the region — an advantage over nonintegrated refineries in the region.

Same connection, different wellhead

Across Oklahoma and Kansas, gas plants, gathering systems and pipelines extend that network, bringing natural gas and natural gas liquids, or NGLs, from the field to customers and markets.

Gather: The journey begins at the wellhead, where natural gas is collected.

Process: It is then separated into NGLs, including ethane, propane and butane.

Deliver: The natural gas then moves to customers, while NGLs move to markets such as heating, cooking, manufacturing, petrochemicals and gasoline blending.

Together, those connected assets help move the right products to the right customers and markets.

Ensuring reliability through our own products

Integration is also about putting our own products to work across the system. Phillips 66’s lubricant products help keep the pumps, compressors and other equipment that support midstream operations running smoothly.

The Phillips 66 Hartford Lubricants Plant in Illinois is a primary packaging and distribution hub for lubricant products used across various industries, including automakers, equipment manufacturers, power generation, agriculture and mining.

From the inland to the West Coast

Looking ahead, the Central Corridor is expected to supply Western Gateway, extending the reach of this connected system to Arizona, Nevada and California.

Illinois: An example of integration in motion

In 2025, Phillips 66 acquired the remaining 50% interest in WRB Refining LP, bringing Wood River Refinery and Borger Refinery fully under company ownership. The move strengthened Phillips 66’s position in a region where it already had scale, supply connectivity and strong customer relationships.

Chicago looks good in orange

The Wood River Refinery connects refining, midstream, marketing, aviation and commercial capabilities and gives Phillips 66 direct access to major Midwest demand centers, including Chicago.

In a region with a strong Phillips 66® and Conoco® brand presence, marketing has introduced the 76® brand in Chicago, successfully growing the brand’s presence in a new market.

Connecting aviation supply

The Wood River Refinery supplies aviation fuel — both jet and sustainable aviation fuel — directly to Chicago O’Hare International Airport through an established pipeline.

Under an agreement with United Airlines, SAF from the Rodeo Renewable Energy Complex in California is transported to the region, blended with conventional jet fuel produced at Wood River and delivered to O’Hare.

This agreement highlights the connectivity of the entire integrated system and logistics capabilities, moving product from the West Coast to the Central Corridor.

Nationwide, Phillips 66 Aviation supplies 10% of the nation’s jet fuel demand and operates one of the largest branded FBO networks, with a strong presence in this region.

The integration advantage

No single refinery, gas plant, pipeline, terminal or commercial office alone creates Phillips 66’s Central Corridor advantage. The connections between them create flexibility, supply reliability, expanded market access and the ability to respond quickly when conditions change.

This support from the UK Government is not only backing Catagen as a great business, but also Northern Ireland’s skilled workforce, helping the region remain at the cutting-edge of sustainable aviation and technology.

The backing from UKEF has been instrumental in bridging the gap between late-stage product development and commercialisation. title: Investing Through the Sustainability Cycle | GIC ThinkSpace
description:

Investing in a structural theme requires two things: identifying its long-term direction and assessing where the theme sits within the market cycle (Exhibit 3).
The other side of physical risk—adaptation as an investible opportunity The world must prepare for a harsher climate.
Transition policy is more exposed to the electoral and budgetary cycle, as changes to the Inflation Reduction Act (IRA) and the shift in European sentiment discussed above illustrate.
Adaptation policy behaves differently.
text:
On current policies, climate scientists expect global warming to reach +2.8°C above pre-industrial levels by 2100, almost double today’s warming of +1.4°C2. Climate disasters and associated costs are already rising at alarming rates, but extreme weather will become more frequent and severe than what we experience today.

The implication for investors is clear. Climate change depends on physics. Physical risks accrue regardless of political or market sentiment, and they cut two ways: they are exposures we must underwrite, and they are the demand driver behind an adaptation opportunity set whose growth is anchored in the same physics.

Transition risks, arising from the world’s shift to a low-carbon economy, are different in character: they are cyclical, ebbing and flowing with financial markets, policy, and the economics of green technology. It is precisely this cyclicality that makes the transition so easy to misread in the short term.

Long-term investing requires looking past these swings to understand how both types of risk affect investments and where they open new opportunities. Yet clarity of direction is not enough. Investing in a structural theme requires two things: identifying its long-term direction and assessing where the theme sits within the market cycle (Exhibit 3).

Reading the transition cycle—what markets, policy, and technology show

The direction of physical risk is not in doubt—the science and the loss data are clear, and it will intensify regardless of sentiment. The questions are centred on the transition: how fast, how far, and where the economics hold.

To gauge where transition risk sits in the cycle, we anchor on data and empirical evidence, examining three forces that drive it—financial markets, policy on the ground, and green technology economics—which together point to a transition that is uneven and cyclical, yet structurally intact.

What are financial markets saying

Global clean energy stocks—iShares Global Clean Energy ETF (ICLN)—have outperformed the MSCI All Country World Index (ACWI) by 29 percentage points since 1 January 2025 (Exhibit 4), despite a softening of policy support in some markets. While higher interest rates weighed down clean energy share prices from 2022-2025, recent AI-driven electricity demand has served as a positive catalyst, lifting the outlook for all forms of energy, and creating favourable conditions for clean energy to pick up. This is why understanding where we are in the cycle is important for investors.

The other side of physical risk—adaptation as an investible opportunity

The world must prepare for a harsher climate. Adaptation will need to scale across society to strengthen the resilience of economies and communities to physical climate risks. Governments, businesses, and households all need ways to manage more extreme heat, floods, droughts, and storms. Companies that provide these solutions will play an increasingly important role in helping economies and communities thrive as physical risks intensify.

In our May 2025 research paper4, produced with Bain & Company’s support, we estimated that global annual revenues from a select set of adaptation solutions will grow from US$1tn today to US$4tn by 2050 in our Base Case. The corresponding investment opportunity across public and private debt and equity is estimated to rise from US$2tn today to US$9tn by 2050, of which US$3tn is incremental growth attributable to global warming.

Critically, the size of that opportunity proved largely resilient to the climate pathway that ultimately unfolds, varying only around 4% across projections, which means investors can build conviction here without having to forecast the precise climate outcome.

Three features make this opportunity set distinctive.

A different risk profile: mature businesses, not technology bets

The adaptation universe consists of many companies that are already profitable, with proven products, established customers, and functioning distribution. Weather-resilient building materials, water infrastructure, industrial cooling, and drainage are not venture propositions awaiting a cost-curve breakthrough. Relative to parts of the transition opportunity set, the investment case therefore carries materially less commercial and technology risk: the question is not whether the product works or whether it can reach cost parity, but how quickly demand compounds and whether the industry structure allows that demand to be captured profitably.

Climate elasticity of demand: an under-appreciated source of revenue upside

What changes for these businesses in the years ahead is not their technology, but their demand curve. As physical hazards intensify, the climate elasticity of demand—the degree to which demand for a product responds to worsening climate conditions—should accelerate revenue growth beyond historical trends. It could also lift margins, since climate-resilient variants of established products typically carry higher gross margins than their standard equivalents.

This upside remains poorly reflected in consensus forecasts. Most financial planning and analysis teams and sell-side analysts continue to rely on historical data for forecasting, and this information gap presents long-term investors with an opportunity to invest where company earnings may positively surprise as demand for adaptation solutions increases. Our own estimates put adaptation revenues by 2050 as much as 61% above historical trend-based forecasts5.

The corporate side of this gap is beginning to close. Across 2026 quarterly earnings calls, management teams in several adaptation-exposed sectors have begun attributing a positive demand outlook to climate-driven demand. Building products companies point to tightening regulatory and insurance requirements driving demand for more durable offerings; power equipment firms report stronger demand for backup generation as extreme weather disrupts grids6.

Policy that ratchets rather than reverses

Perhaps the most underrated distinction is policy durability. Transition policy is more exposed to the electoral and budgetary cycle, as changes to the Inflation Reduction Act (IRA) and the shift in European sentiment discussed above illustrate. Adaptation policy behaves differently. Building codes, flood-zone requirements, and resilience standards are typically revised after a damaging event, and rarely loosened. The direction of travel is largely one-way, which gives the demand signal a stickiness that transition-linked demand often lacks. At the macro level, the number of countries and economies with national adaptation plans in place has accelerated markedly (Exhibit 13).

text:
The Brazilian National Civil Aviation Agency (Agência Nacional de Aviação Civil – “ANAC”) has submitted to public consultation a draft Resolution that will regulate the monitoring, reporting and verification (“MRV”) of CO₂ emissions from domestic air operations, as well as the enforcement of compliance with the annual regulatory target for reducing such emissions, under the National Sustainable Aviation Fuel Program (Programa Nacional de Combustível Sustentável de Aviação – “ProBioQAV”). The public consultation will remain open until October 1, 2026.

Under the draft, the Resolution will apply to every air operator that emits 10,000 tonnes of CO₂ or more in a given year and that (i) is certified under Brazilian Civil Aviation Regulation (Regulamento Brasileiro de Aviação Civil – “RBAC”) No. 119; or (ii) operates under RBAC No. 129. The draft further provides that air operators must submit to ANAC an Emissions Monitoring Plan by October 31 of the same year in which they reach, or expect to reach, the 10,000-tonne CO₂ emissions threshold, and must file an Emissions Report annually.

To comply with the annual regulatory emissions reduction target set forth in Article 10 of Law No. 14,993/2024 (the “Fuel of the Future Law”)—which starts at 1% as of January 1, 2027, and reaches 10% as of January 1, 2037—operators must retire SAF Sustainability Certificates (Certificados de Sustentabilidade do SAF – “CS-SAF”). The target may be partially met through a combination of the following alternative compliance mechanisms:

The use of Lower Carbon Aviation Fuels (“LCAF”);

Retirement of Decarbonization Credits (Créditos de Descarbonização – “CBIOs”) under the National Biofuels Policy (Política Nacional de Biocombustíveis – RenovaBio);

The use of SAF sustainability certificates originating from other countries, provided that there is a reciprocity agreement with Brazil and that the other applicable requirements are met; and

Verified Emission Reduction or Removal Certificates (Certificados de Redução ou Remoção Verificada de Emissões – CRVE), an asset of the Brazilian Greenhouse Gas Emissions Trading System (Sistema Brasileiro de Comércio de Emissões de Gases de Efeito Estufa – SBCE).

Under the regulatory decree discussed below, the combination of these alternative mechanisms may not exceed 5% of the mandatory annual target, with transitional caps of up to 15% in 2027 and 2028, and up to 10% in 2029.

ANAC opened the public consultation following the publication of Decree No. 13,094 of August 12, 2026 (the “Decree”), which regulates ProBioQAV and establishes the operational rules for the production, certification, trading and oversight of Sustainable Aviation Fuel (“SAF”), as well as for compliance with the mandatory greenhouse gas (“GHG”) emissions reduction targets imposed by the Fuel of the Future Law on air operators in domestic flights.

The program's core instrument is the CS-SAF, a book-entry instrument issued in units corresponding to the volume or mass of SAF demonstrably sold in the domestic market. The CS-SAF allows the environmental attribute to be separated from the physical fuel, so that it can be traded separately from the biofuel molecule under the book & claim model. In practice, the CS-SAF serves as the environmental asset that air operators must retire to demonstrate compliance with the regulatory emissions reduction targets. All SAF sold in Brazil for use in domestic and international flights must be linked to a CS-SAF, which will be valid for 18 months from its issuance for purposes of demonstrating compliance with the target.

For SAF certification, domestic producers may opt for certification either under the National SAF Certification Program (Programa Nacional de Certificação de SAF), to be established by the National Agency of Petroleum, Natural Gas and Biofuels (Agência Nacional do Petróleo, Gás Natural e Biocombustíveis – “ANP”), or in accordance with the criteria and methodologies of the Carbon Offsetting and Reduction Scheme for International Aviation (“CORSIA”) of the International Civil Aviation Organization (“ICAO”), in which case it will automatically be deemed eligible under the national program. Imported SAF, in turn, must be certified in accordance with CORSIA requirements. Notably, the Decree expressly prohibits the issuance of CBIOs for SAF production, in order to prevent double counting of the environmental benefit associated with the fuel. This prohibition does not, however, prevent air operators from using CBIOs as an alternative mechanism to comply with the target, subject to the limits described above.

ANAC will oversee compliance with the targets, and operators must complete the retirement of CS-SAFs in the volume required to meet their targets by January 31 of the year following the target reference year.

In light of this scenario, air operators, SAF producers and importers, and other players in the value chain should assess the impacts of the new rules on their supply and compliance strategies, bearing in mind that the first reduction target will apply as of January 1, 2027, and that ANP and ANAC must issue their complementary regulations—including those governing the National SAF Certification Program—by December 18, 2026. In this context, the public consultation provides a relevant opportunity for regulated entities to contribute to the design of the MRV rules and the penalty regime before their approval.

The Environmental, Climate Change and Sustainability practice of Tauil & Chequer Advogados in association with Mayer Brown remains available to provide further clarification on the obligations and opportunities related to ProBioQAV.

title: SABA Members' New Purchasing Agreement for Next-Gen SAF | Procurement Magazine
description:
In an announcement made by Sustainable Aviation Buyers Alliance (SABA), the alliance’s members have committed to purchasing sustainable aviation fuel certificates (SAFc) associated with Infinium Energy’s Project Atlas.
A new approach to SAF procurement SABA’s latest procurement was supported by its leading member organisations such as AVEVA, Bain & Company, Google and McKinsey, marking an important addition to its market model.
SABA’s next-generation SAF procurement was designed to drive investment into innovative technologies needed to bring scalable supply to the market in the years to come.
Corporate customers investing in SAF SABA procurements use a book and claim model that allows corporate customers to invest in SAF and claim associated environmental benefits – even when the fuel doesn’t flow directly into their planes.
