text:
The scope of the commercial agreement between Plug Power and Arcadia eFuels – the Danish start-up, which has, however, relocated its headquarters to Austin, Texas – has been significantly expanded. The company specialises in the construction of plants for the production of synthetic aviation fuels, known as eSAFs.

As announced by the US company, the parties have in fact signed a new agreement – following the one signed in 2023 regarding the plant to be built at the port of Vordingborg in Denmark – which designates Plug as the preferred supplier of PEM electrolysers for a further four plants that the Scandinavian group intends to develop across Europe and the Americas.

According to the statement, the total electrolysis capacity would amount to over 1 GW and would be in addition to the 280 MW planned for the Danish project, known as ENDOR, for which the completion timeline has since been extended beyond the 2023 forecast. The FID was scheduled for 2024, whilst production was expected to commence in 2026.

The new press release does not specify an updated deadline for the final investment decision and states that deliveries of the electrolysers will commence following formal authorisation to proceed.

In the meantime, Arcadia has nevertheless found a buyer for part of its future output. The German energy group Uniper, in fact, has committed to purchasing 40,000 tonnes of e-SAF per year from the Danish plant. The contract covers a period of more than 10 years and provides for deliveries to begin in the early years of the next decade.

Once completed, the Vordingborg plant will use electricity generated from wind power to produce, via Plug’s electrolysis system, around 110 tonnes of green hydrogen per day. The H2 it will then be combined with CO2 captured to produce eSAF.

“The agreement extends our collaboration with Arcadia eFuels from ENDOR to other plants that will be built in Europe and the Americas in the future, confirming confidence in our technology and our ability to deliver projects of this scale,” commented José Luis Crespo, Chairman and Chief Executive Officer of Plug. “European aviation fuel mandates are driving demand for e-SAFs. Producing them using electricity and CO2 ”of European origin also helps to strengthen the continent’s energy security by reducing dependence on imported oil’.

“The contract with Plug is one of the agreements already finalised as part of the process leading up to the final investment decision for ENDOR,” added Amy Hebert, Chief Executive of Arcadia eFuels. “To achieve aviation’s decarbonisation targets, we will need fuels produced from renewable hydrogen and captured CO₂. Plug has the experience and supply capacity required for our plant, as well as the reliability demanded by our financiers.”.

title: Vertical Aerospace has already started work on its hybrid-electric demonstrator
description:
Now, the same Vertical Aerospace VX4 prototype sits dismantled inside a hangar at Cotswold Airport, preparing for a second life.
Key to this is the integration of a secondary fuel system, and for G-EVTA, this means removing several battery packs to make way for a gas turbine, generator and fuel system.
Vertical hopes to begin flight testing with the hybrid electric demonstrator early in 2027.
Airport availability also complicated the proposed return flight, making road transport the more practical way to get the hybrid work started.
These are development targets for the future hybrid aircraft rather than capabilities already demonstrated by AC2.
text:
Two months ago, it was flying in front of thousands of people at Farnborough Airshow. Now, the same Vertical Aerospace VX4 prototype sits dismantled inside a hangar at Cotswold Airport, preparing for a second life.

During AGN’s visit to the opening of the first production facility for Vertical’s groundbreaking Valo passenger aircraft, engineers explained how they are converting this VX4 prototype into a hybrid-electric demonstrator.

While Vertical’s core work on building the first Valo continues, the company is looking to move beyond short, fully electric passenger flights into longer-range cargo, commercial and defence operations. Key to this is the integration of a secondary fuel system, and for G-EVTA, this means removing several battery packs to make way for a gas turbine, generator and fuel system.

At the back of the company’s newly opened Aircraft Assembly Centre, the aircraft known internally as AC2 offered a very different sight from its Farnborough flying display. Its disassembled state was evidence of the next phase already getting under way.

Vertical hopes to begin flight testing with the hybrid electric demonstrator early in 2027.

Why Vertical’s Farnborough aircraft came home by road

AC2 had completed close to 90 flights, according to production manager Ellis, including numerous full piloted transitions that prepared it to fly repeatedly at Farnborough.

Its newer counterpart, Aircraft Three, is now continuing the all-electric flight-test campaign. That frees the earlier aircraft for conversion while Vertical keeps gathering flight data.

Despite having demonstrated its capabilities in the air, AC2 returned from Farnborough by road. The team explained that preparing Aircraft Three for its flight campaign had taken priority. Airport availability also complicated the proposed return flight, making road transport the more practical way to get the hybrid work started.

“We wanted to start [the] hybrid programme sooner,” Ellis said.

Dismantling the aircraft for transport also fit the work that awaited it at Kemble. Rather than get it all prepared for a ferry flight only to then take it apart again, the team could proceed towards the modification before AC2 even left Farnborough.

The aircraft took around three or four days to break down into subassemblies. When AGN visited, the team was inspecting its components ahead of the conversion.

How the VX4 is becoming a hybrid-electric aircraft

The biggest change will be how the aircraft obtains its electrical energy.

The conversion removes four of its eight battery packs. A gas turbine and generator will be installed within the fuselage, with a fuel tank behind them, while the remaining batteries continue to form part of the power system.

The propellers will still be driven by electric motors. The turbine’s role is to generate electricity, rather than mechanically turn the propellers.

“The batteries, the HV cables to the motors remain the same,” Ellis explained. “That whole architecture is exactly the same as it was.”

Some existing structure will be removed and new structure installed to support the engine. The team will also receive additional training for working with the fuel system.

Asked whether the integration presented any particularly daunting challenges, Ellis was relaxed about the work ahead. The technicians already have experience building and modifying Vertical’s prototypes, while a complete hybrid powertrain is being tested separately on the ground.

One detail remained firmly under wraps. When AGN asked who was supplying the turbine, the answer was brief: “Wait and see.”

Ground testing prepares the hybrid for flight

Although the dismantled aircraft makes the programme newly tangible, Vertical has been developing its hybrid technology for several years.

The company announced the programme in May 2025. A year later, it reported that integration testing had begun on its Hybrid Propulsion Evaluation Rig, known as HYPER, following more than two years of development.

The rig allows engineers to test the turbine, generator, electrical systems and controls together, including how they respond to faults, before installing the system in an aircraft.

Vertical has described the turbine as compatible with sustainable aviation fuel. The hybrid will nevertheless burn fuel, bringing a different operating and emissions profile from the fully electric Valo.

During the tour, the team said the work now centres on fitting that tested system into the prototype, including the structural changes needed for the installation.

Why Vertical wants greater range and payload

Vertical’s ambitions for the eventual hybrid variant are considerably greater than those of its electric passenger aircraft.

The company is targeting a range of up to 1,000 miles – approximately 870 nm – and configurations carrying up to 1,100 kg. These are development targets for the future hybrid aircraft rather than capabilities already demonstrated by AC2.

For Stuart Simpson, Vertical’s CEO, that additional capability creates opportunities beyond the short journeys envisaged for the all-electric Valo.

“The hybrid then opens up new opportunities with increased range, and it also opens it up for military opportunities for distributed logistics, where they want to be able to carry a much higher payload,” he said.

The aim is to serve more markets using shared aircraft technology. Electric passenger services, longer commercial journeys and military resupply have different requirements, but Vertical believes variants of its platform can address them without starting each design from scratch.

The fully electric aircraft remains the immediate certification priority. All seven Valos planned for the initial certification programme will be electric, with UK type certification targeted for 2029. The hybrid demonstrator’s planned flights in the first half of 2027 will support a separate development effort.

For AC2, the next public appearance could therefore look familiar while concealing a substantial change inside. The aircraft that helped demonstrate electric transition flight at Farnborough is now being rebuilt to explore how far that technology can travel with a turbine aboard.

text:
After more than a century in business, Coast Packing is finding that what’s old is new again.

On a recent episode of The Food Institute Podcast, guest host Justin D’Affronte of City National Bank spoke with Coast Packing chairman and CEO Eric Gustafson about the company’s 104 year family legacy, renewed consumer interest in lard and beef tallow, and the economic pressures facing food manufacturers in California.

Founded by Gustafson’s great-grandfather and his business partner in 1922, Coast Packing began as a full-line slaughter and meatpacking facility in Vernon, California. When changing economics led the company to exit slaughter operations in the 1960s, it pivoted toward products it had previously produced as byproducts: lard and tallow.

That decision ultimately established Coast Packing’s modern identity as a specialist in animal fat shortenings.

Today, Gustafson represents the fourth generation of his family to lead the business.

“I’m very fortunate and blessed to be the fourth-generation CEO and chairman,” Gustafson said. “Certainly didn’t come easy and still isn’t, but I feel very fortunate [and] honored that I’m trusted by my family and my employees to lead this business forward.”

Animal Fats Come Full Circle

One of the biggest changes Gustafson has witnessed during his 16-plus years as CEO is a shift in how consumers perceive animal fats.

After decades in which lard, tallow, and saturated fats faced scrutiny, he feels consumers have become increasingly interested in natural and minimally processed ingredients. That movement has helped generate new interest in Coast Packing’s core products.

“It’s fun to see things come full circle with these consumer trends that are supporting our business again,” Gustafson said. Lard and tallow serve different culinary purposes.

Lard, which comes from pork fat, remains prominent in applications such as tamales, flour tortillas, baked goods and pie crusts. Tallow, derived from beef fat, is particularly suited to heavy-duty frying.

Gustafson pointed to growing restaurant interest in beef tallow for French fries, arguing that it can offer advantages in taste, texture and operational performance.

For foodservice operators, he said tallow can also provide longer fry life and require less cleaning than some alternatives. Coast Packing generally sees customers achieve at least a 50% reduction in frying-oil usage when switching to tallow, according to Gustafson.

California Manufacturing Challenges

While Coast Packing remains deeply rooted in Southern California, Gustafson expressed concern about the difficulty of operating a manufacturing business in the state.

“I love California, born and raised,” he said, but added that its regulatory environment has “made it more challenging to operate here as a manufacturer.”

Those challenges extend to sourcing. While Coast Packing continues to work with suppliers in Central California, Gustafson said the majority of its raw materials now come from the Midwest and other parts of the country.

He argued that higher regulatory and operating costs ultimately reach consumers, either through the price of locally manufactured goods or the expense associated with transporting products into California from elsewhere.

Labor presents another challenge – and responsibility. Gustafson emphasized that Coast Packing’s longevity depends on building a culture in which employees and the business succeed together.

“If there’s no employees, there’s no Coast Packing,” he said. “But without Coast Packing, you won’t have employees.”

Commodity Markets Add Pressure

Beyond regulation and labor, Coast Packing must navigate volatile commodity markets.

Gustafson explained that food producers increasingly compete for fats and oils with renewable diesel and sustainable aviation fuel manufacturers. Changes in crude-oil markets and government incentives for renewable fuels can therefore ripple into the price of edible fats.

At the same time, tight U.S. cattle supplies put additional pressure on the tallow market. With fewer animals available and multiple industries competing for raw materials, basic supply-and demand dynamics can quickly push costs higher.

Despite those pressures, Coast Packing is looking to capitalize on renewed interest in its century-old product categories. The company’s website now offers recipes, educational resources, “Taste Maps” identifying restaurants and bakeries that use lard and tallow, and a beef tallow savings calculator for foodservice operators.

For a company founded in 1922, changing consumer tastes may ultimately be bringing Coast Packing back to where it started: making traditional ingredients relevant to a new generation.

text:
Brazil's state-controlled oil company is turning to blockchain technology to bring more accountability to the market for lower-carbon fuels. Petrobras has developed two research applications on the Cardano network to track environmental claims tied to sustainable aviation fuel and its partly renewable diesel product, the Cardano Foundation announced Wednesday.

The projects, built in partnership with Ledger Labs at the Pontifical Catholic University of Rio de Janeiro (PUC-Rio), aim to solve a structural problem in how green fuel attributes are bought and sold. One application, called CS-SAF, tokenizes the environmental benefits of certified jet fuel. The other creates digital checkpoints to trace the journey of Diesel R, Petrobras' renewable diesel, from production through consumption.

"Brazil has been one of the most consistent adopters of Cardano, from SERPRO in government to SENAI in industry," said Frederik Gregaard, chief executive of the Cardano Foundation. "It's great to see Petrobras, one of the largest firms in the region, continue to see value in on-chain provenance and traceability."

The aviation project addresses a specific weakness in the sustainable fuel market. Under what is known as a book-and-claim model, an airline can pay for the environmental benefit of sustainable aviation fuel even when the physical product is delivered elsewhere. That separation creates an accounting challenge: without a reliable registry, two different companies could potentially claim the same emissions reduction.

CS-SAF attempts to close that gap by issuing digital tokens on Cardano that represent certified sustainability attributes. Before any token is minted, the platform verifies that the underlying fuel meets the requirements of CORSIA, the Carbon Offsetting and Reduction Scheme for International Aviation established by the International Civil Aviation Organization. Once a buyer makes a claim, the corresponding token is permanently retired on-chain, preventing reuse.

The system also includes a passenger-facing application. Travelers can enter their departure and destination airports, calculate the fuel benefit associated with their journey, and receive a digital certificate linking their allocation back to the original fuel certificate. Petrobras produces its sustainable aviation fuel at the Duque de Caxias refinery through co-processing petroleum inputs with renewable materials.

The second application takes a different approach, focusing on traceability rather than claim management. It would record information at each stage of Diesel R's production, transportation and use, assembling those records into a complete history of the fuel's journey. The Cardano Foundation said such data could support Scope 3 emissions reporting, which covers indirect emissions across a company's value chain — information that often resides with suppliers and customers rather than the reporting company itself.

Petrobras markets Diesel R in versions with different renewable content, including R5 at 5% and R10 at 10%. The varying renewable shares underscore why precise records matter: a fuel's renewable content, its calculated lifecycle emissions, and the benefit a buyer may report are distinct pieces of information that auditors need to verify independently.

Both projects remain firmly in the research phase. The diesel model is described as proposed, and the announcement disclosed neither the fuel volumes covered by the applications nor a timeline for broader deployment. The public case study also does not identify participating airline customers or report how many sustainability claims have been retired through the system.

Certification remains the governing authority for sustainable fuel claims. Petrobras' aviation fuel has received CORSIA sustainability certification through recognized frameworks, which require detailed evidence of feedstocks, production methods, and lifecycle carbon emissions. A blockchain record can help trace a certificate after it is issued, but it does not replace the comprehensive certification process required for regulatory compliance.

"Institutional interest in Cardano keeps growing, especially with x402 arriving on Cardano and Fireblocks adding support for Cardano Native Tokens," Gregaard added. "It's never been a better time for enterprises to consider what this technology offers."

The collaboration between Petrobras and the Cardano Foundation began in 2023 with blockchain education for the energy company's employees. It expanded in 2025 to include energy-sector research with PUC-Rio's Ledger Labs.

Petrobras is not alone in exploring blockchain for sustainable fuel accounting. Shell launched Avelia, a book-and-claim platform, in 2022. In a September update, the energy major said Avelia had contributed to more than 84 million gallons of sustainable aviation fuel entering the global fuel network since its launch, resulting in more than 780,000 tonnes of CO2e abatement through June 2026. Australia's Viva Energy signed an agreement with NoviqTech in January to research digital book-and-claim systems for sustainable aviation fuel.

The practical measure of success for Petrobras' initiative will be whether the system makes certificate reconciliation faster, gives auditors sufficient evidence, and interoperates with other registries. Documented results on those points would strengthen the case for adopting blockchain-based tracking across the broader fuel supply chain. For now, the projects represent a notable test of whether distributed ledger technology can bring greater transparency to the increasingly complex market for lower-carbon fuels.

text:
Petrobras, Brazil’s state-controlled energy company, has built two research-stage blockchain applications on Cardano to record the environmental claims tied to its sustainable aviation fuel and renewable diesel, the Cardano Foundation announced on Wednesday.

Both came out of a research and development partnership between Petrobras, the Swiss not-for-profit Cardano Foundation and Rio de Janeiro’s Pontifical Catholic University (PUC-Rio). The goal is to make emissions and fuel lifecycle data easier to check, as airlines and passengers look for ways to verify green fuel claims.

Get Unchained’s crypto news in your inbox with the free Unchained Daily newsletter.

One Credit, One Claim

The first tool covers sustainable aviation fuel (SAF), a lower-carbon jet fuel that works in existing aircraft and airport infrastructure. It runs on a Book-and-Claim model, which splits the fuel’s environmental benefit from the physical fuel so that the benefit can be credited to an airline, company or traveler even if the fuel was produced or used somewhere else.

According to the foundation’s case study, each SAF attribute is issued on Cardano as a standardized token called CS-SAF, with metadata aligned to CORSIA, the carbon offsetting scheme for international aviation. The tokens can be minted, transferred and retired, which is meant to stop the same benefit from being counted twice.

Passengers can type in their departure and arrival airports, work out the matching CS-SAF amount and receive a certificate showing their route, distance and allocation, linked to the original fuel certificate.

Tracking Diesel R

The second tool targets Diesel R, Petrobras’ renewable diesel brand, and was built with PUC-Rio. The foundation described it as a proposed model that logs checkpoints as the fuel is produced, transported and used, building a single record of its lifecycle.

That record is aimed at Scope 3 reporting, which covers indirect emissions across a company’s value chain and often depends on data held by suppliers and logistics firms.

“The energy transition will depend as much on trust as it does on new fuels,” said Rafael Fraga, LATAM business development lead at the Cardano Foundation. “Public blockchain gives us the opportunity to make that trust part of the system by design.”

The announcement did not give a timeline for commercial rollout of either tool.

From Training to Traceability

The work extends a relationship that started in December 2023, when the Cardano Foundation agreed to run blockchain education workshops for Petrobras staff through Petrobras University, a program open to more than 40,000 employees. In April 2025, the foundation announced a research collaboration with PUC-Rio’s Ledger Labs that would focus first on blockchain uses for renewable fuels, with Petrobras as an industry partner.

title: US scientists develop catalyst to turn woody biomass into jet fuel components
description:

text:
A Rowan University research team is investigating how woody biomass could replace petroleum-derived components in aviation fuel, helping reduce the United States’ dependence on fossil fuels for flight.

The project focuses on lignin, a natural polymer found in woody biomass, and a catalyst designed to convert selected molecules into aromatic compounds suitable for jet fuel.

Jun Hee Jang, an assistant professor of chemical engineering at the Henry M. Rowan College of Engineering, received a $199,999 National Science Foundation grant to investigate the process and assess its economic potential.

Replacing petroleum-derived fuel components

Aviation fuel contains a blend of compounds, including linear hydrocarbons, branched hydrocarbons, and aromatics.

Producing sustainable alternatives requires addressing these different components rather than replacing the entire blend with a single substance.

Researchers have already established processes for converting biomass, including vegetable oils, into hydrocarbons. Aromatic compounds, however, are typically sourced from petroleum, leaving an opportunity to develop renewable alternatives.

Jang’s research examines whether lignin can supply those aromatics. The work forms part of broader efforts to expand sustainable aviation fuel production using renewable resources and reduce reliance on petroleum-based aviation fuel through 2050.

If successful, the approach could support domestic fuel production while adding value to unused biomass feedstocks.

More from Energy

See All

The project targets aviation fuel components, with the catalyst’s performance and the process’s commercial viability still to be evaluated.

A catalyst that selects by size

Before lignin can be converted into useful fuel components, researchers must break it into smaller molecules. That step produces a mixture containing molecules of different sizes.

Some smaller molecules can be upgraded into aviation fuel components, while larger molecules cannot undergo the same conversion. Efficiently separating these groups presents a central challenge for the research team.

Jang and his colleagues plan to develop a size-selective catalyst with a porous structure that admits smaller molecules while preventing larger ones from entering.

Inside those pores, the smaller molecules can be converted into jet fuel-range aromatic compounds. The design therefore aims to control which parts of the mixture reach the catalyst’s conversion sites.

Meanwhile, the larger molecules remain outside the porous structure, preserving properties that could make them useful in other applications.

Turning potential waste into another product

In conventional catalytic processes, the larger molecules can become waste products. Jang’s approach instead seeks to retain them as potentially valuable co-products alongside the fuel aromatics.

“By applying this catalyst, we can produce not only fuel aromatics, but also larger molecules that could have further functional applications,” Jang said.

One doctoral student and one postdoctoral researcher will join Jang on the project.

The postdoctoral researcher brings experience in designing chemical synthesis methods, while the doctoral student will conduct experiments and analyze the resulting products.

Together, they will investigate how catalyst design affects reaction performance and evaluate the economics of scaling the proposed biomass-to-aviation fuel process.

text:
Metro Atlanta Chamber, Georgia Farm Bureau, Georgia Forestry Association and Delta Air Lines Launch Georgia SAF Coalition

ATLANTA, Sept. 30, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- Georgia agriculture and forestry producers and the business community have teamed up to create the Georgia Sustainable Aviation Fuel (SAF) Coalition, a new partnership focused on positioning the state as a national leader in sustainable aviation fuel research and production. Founding organizations include the Metro Atlanta Chamber, Georgia Farm Bureau, Georgia Forestry Association, and Delta Air Lines, working together to accelerate domestic production of biofuels that utilize Georgia grown agriculture and forestry feedstocks.

Sustainable aviation fuel can be produced from a variety of feedstocks to reduce emissions from air transportation and is designed to be compatible with existing aircraft and fueling infrastructure. While SAF currently represents a small share of global fuel supply, demand is rising quickly across global markets as production scales and interest from airlines and customers continues to accelerate.

Thanks to strong political and business leadership, Georgia has built a foundation to grow the capacity needed to produce ag- and forestry-derived SAF. The Georgia SAF Coalition aims to accelerate that growth by better coordinating public-private partnerships, more closely aligning university research with industry needs, and considering avenues to attract investment.

The coalition's launch builds on the momentum of Georgia's Keep Georgia Forested Act, which encourages investment in forestry manufacturing, including the production of biofuels from Georgia-based feedstocks. The legislation, signed into law by Gov. Brian Kemp in May 2026, enhances Georgia's competitiveness by allowing certain tax credits to be transferred. This change allows companies to monetize credits during the critical early stages of construction and operations, when workers are being hired and capital needs are highest. That investment reaches beyond aviation, creating new markets for Georgia farmers and forest landowners and sustaining demand for locally grown feedstocks.

Georgia's combination of agriculture and forestry resources, world-class research institutions, logistics infrastructure, and industry leadership positions the state to become a leader in sustainable aviation fuel development and production.

"This is about aligning Georgia's natural strengths with real market demand," said Katie Kirkpatrick, President and CEO of the Metro Atlanta Chamber. "Georgia is making a serious play for a piece of the emerging sustainable aviation fuel market. By bringing global companies, producers, researchers, and the agricultural community all to the same table, we are building a powerful biofuels ecosystem that serves the entire state and connects us to the world."

"For farmers across Georgia, sustainable aviation fuel could open new markets for our agricultural commodities, offering new opportunities and increased profitability," said Tom McCall, President of Georgia Farm Bureau. "Partnerships like the Georgia SAF Coalition help connect broader economic innovation to agriculture, the number one industry in our state."

"Georgia is the number one forestry state in the nation, and our state's 22 million acres of working forests are among the most productive in the world," said Tim Lowrimore, President & CEO, Georgia Forestry Association. "SAF provides a chance to put that resource to work in a growing market which means new demand for landowners, new jobs in rural Georgia and new manufacturing investment in the communities that need it most. This coalition makes sure producers are at the table from day one."

"Georgia is well positioned to become a national leader in SAF," said Peter Carter, President of Delta Air Lines. "The Georgia SAF Coalition unites organizations committed to advancing that opportunity. Together, we can power the growth of a SAF industry that strengthens Georgia's economy, supports innovation, and creates lasting benefits for communities across the state."

"Sustainable aviation fuel represents a significant opportunity for the nation's agricultural and forestry sectors and the rural communities that support them. The Georgia SAF Coalition brings together producers, industry leaders and other stakeholders to help unlock new markets, drive innovation and strengthen American energy leadership. Georgia has the resources and expertise to play an important role in the future of SAF while creating economic opportunities across the state. I am glad to see the public-private partnerships behind the effort to allow Sustainable Aviation Fuel to take flight," said Stephen Vaden, Deputy Secretary, U.S. Department of Agriculture.

Prior to launch, coalition members joined the Georgia Research Alliance in successfully advocating for state funding for a Georgia Research Alliance Eminent Scholar. This research will focus on the forestry sector and help identify emerging opportunities, including biofuels.

Founding members of the Georgia SAF Coalition include Delta Air Lines, Georgia Farm Bureau, Georgia Forestry Association, and the Metro Atlanta Chamber. Anchor partners include Boeing, Cox Enterprises, and Norfolk Southern, with additional support from supporting partners RYAM and Gulfstream Aerospace.

Research, education and community partners include the Georgia Institute of Technology, Georgia Research Alliance, Georgia Southern University, Technical College System of Georgia, University of Georgia, Clean Cities Georgia, Georgia Agribusiness Council, Georgia Association of Manufacturers, Hartsfield-Jackson Atlanta International Airport, and the National Federation of Independent Business.

The coalition's immediate priorities are: recruiting SAF and biofuels facilities to Georgia, connecting university research to industry needs, and building the supply chain that links Georgia's forests and farms to aviation customers.

Learn more or join the coalition at gasaf.org.

text:
Moeve and Emerita Resources have signed Spain’s first agreement to deploy 100% renewable diesel, or HVO, at industrial scale in the mining sector.

The fuel is expected to cut around 2,600 metric tons of CO2 emissions annually at Emerita’s Iberian Belt West project in Huelva.

Moeve and Apical are investing $1.36 billion in a new Huelva biofuels plant with capacity for 500,000 metric tons of HVO and sustainable aviation fuel annually.

Spain targets mining emissions with renewable diesel

Moeve and Emerita Resources are bringing renewable diesel into Spanish mining at industrial scale, targeting one of the harder areas of heavy industry to decarbonize.

Under the agreement, Moeve will become the preferred supplier of hydrotreated vegetable oil, or HVO, to Emerita’s Iberian Belt West mining project in Huelva. The companies said it is the first agreement of its kind in Spain.

The second-generation biofuel can reduce lifecycle CO2 emissions by up to 90% compared with conventional diesel. Crucially for mining operators, HVO can also be used in existing diesel engines. That allows companies to reduce emissions without immediately replacing heavy equipment or transport fleets.

Moeve produces the fuel at its Palos de la Frontera facility in Huelva.

At Iberian Belt West, it will power heavy machinery during construction and subsequent mining operations. It will also be used for heavy-duty transport of mineral concentrates.

The companies estimate the switch could avoid around 2,600 metric tons of CO2 emissions each year. They compare that reduction with the annual carbon absorption of approximately 170,000 trees.

An immediate option for hard-to-electrify operations

Mining faces a difficult decarbonization challenge because its operations depend heavily on energy-intensive machinery and long-distance transport. Electrification can reduce emissions in some applications, but technical and infrastructure constraints remain for heavy equipment.

Renewable diesel offers operators an alternative that can be deployed using existing engines and distribution infrastructure.

“Accelerating the decarbonization of heavy industry is one of Moeve’s key strategic priorities, and to achieve this, we need forward-thinking partners. The agreement reached with Emerita demonstrates that the energy transition can go hand in hand with competitiveness by leveraging 2G biofuels as an immediate solution for the decarbonization of sectors that are difficult to electrify.” Carlos Barrasa, executive vice president of Commercial & Clean Energies at Moeve.

RELATED ARTICLE: Moeve Starts $1.2 Billion Green Hydrogen Project

Emerita CEO Joaquin Merino said the agreement is “fully aligned with Emerita’s environmental DNA.” He added that the Huelva development “is the ideal partner for this Moeve project as an example of sustainable mining.”

For mining executives, the project offers a practical case study in reducing operational emissions without waiting for full fleet electrification. It also places greater attention on lifecycle emissions, fuel sourcing and the availability of lower-carbon alternatives within industrial supply chains.

Huelva builds a local low-carbon industrial ecosystem

The partnership also has a regional industrial dimension. Renewable fuel production, mining operations and mineral export infrastructure are all located within Huelva.

That proximity could reduce logistical complexity while creating a more integrated value chain between energy production, resource extraction and exports.

Moeve is expanding that local supply base further. Together with partner Apical, the company is developing a new second-generation biofuels plant in Huelva.

The project carries a cumulative investment of $1.36 billion and is expected to provide flexible annual production capacity of 500,000 metric tons of HVO and sustainable aviation fuel.

Once operational, the facility will form part of what Moeve describes as the largest second-generation biofuels complex in southern Europe. It supports the company’s ambition to reach 2.5 million metric tons of annual biofuel production capacity by 2030 and lead the Iberian market.

For investors and industrial operators, the Huelva model illustrates how decarbonization investment can increasingly intersect with regional industrial strategy. Local fuel production can support mining and transport operations while reducing dependence on conventional fossil diesel.

The broader significance extends beyond Spain. Mining remains central to supplying minerals required for infrastructure and the energy transition itself. Reducing the operational footprint of extraction will therefore remain a key ESG challenge as demand for those materials grows.

Huelva’s emerging cluster provides one approach: combine local renewable fuel production with heavy industrial demand and existing export infrastructure. If the model proves commercially competitive at scale, it could offer a pathway for other mining regions where electrification remains technically or economically difficult.

For travelers who aren’t willing or able to give up flying, there are ways to reduce the impact of individual trips.
New platforms like BookBetter are helping travelers not only do that research, but also make a tangible impact on reducing future CO2 emissions caused by aviation.
Travelers can compare routes and book flights directly on the platform, and have the option to purchase a contribution toward additional sustainable aviation fuel (SAF).

text:
Being able to fly to any place you wish, at any time you want, is an unbelievable feat of science and engineering. But that magic comes with a trade-off that’s often all too easy to ignore.

For perspective, a transatlantic round-trip flight can generate roughly as much CO₂ per economy passenger as a typical American car emits in about two months, depending on the route and aircraft, according to calculations using data from the International Civil Aviation Organization and U.S. Environmental Protection Agency. Aviation is also responsible for close to four percent of observed, human-induced global warming to date, according to a 2021 study published in the journal Environmental Research Letters. And don’t discount the effects of short-haul flights either. Data from the International Council on Clean Transportation shows that short domestic flights can be among the most carbon-intensive flights per mile, as much of the fuel is burned during takeoff and climb, before a plane reaches efficient cruising altitude.

For travelers who aren’t willing or able to give up flying, there are ways to reduce the impact of individual trips. New platforms like BookBetter are helping travelers not only do that research, but also make a tangible impact on reducing future CO2 emissions caused by aviation.

BookBetter is a travel booking platform that gives users a clear picture of the environmental impact of their flight choices by outlining a route’s contrail impact (aka, condensation trails that form at high altitudes and can trap heat) and carbon emissions per passenger. Travelers can compare routes and book flights directly on the platform, and have the option to purchase a contribution toward additional sustainable aviation fuel (SAF).

SAF is an alternative to conventional jet fuel that, depending on how it is produced, can substantially reduce lifecycle greenhouse-gas emissions. It isn’t a zero-emissions solution: its climate benefit varies by feedstock and production method, supplies remain limited, and purchasing it through a book-and-claim system doesn’t mean the fuel will power your specific flight. But advocates argue that creating additional demand can help scale a technology expected to play an important role in reducing aviation’s reliance on fossil fuel.

SAF purchased on BookBetter doesn’t specifically fuel the plane the traveler will fly on (it isn’t available at every airport), but customers who purchase it do get a certificate that lists a unique ID, the name of the SAF producer, the airport it was delivered to, the volume of emissions reduced, and more, giving travelers as much transparency into their contribution as possible.

“Nicolas Guillaume and I spent years working on alternative fuel for aviation and night trains, watching technical solutions pile up while the actual products for travelers stayed stuck in the past,” Louis Lammertyn, co-founder of BookBetter, told Travel + Leisure, about the inspiration behind the platform. “BookBetter exists because the tools to fly better already exist today. They just weren’t connected to the traveler who could actually use them.”

Lammertyn explained they consciously chose SAF over carbon credits because they believe going directly to the source (aka, the fuel) is “really helping the aviation industry transform.” He noted that this way, you’re physically replacing “fossil kerosene in the fuel system, rather than funding a distant project to compensate by planting trees, while the aviation industry keeps emitting and does not transform. When you book with BookBetter, your contribution to cleaner skies is certified, traceable, and named, not a feel-good rounding error at checkout.”

Of course, BookBetter isn’t alone in trying to make flight emissions more visible when booking. Google Flights has displayed a carbon estimate next to nearly every fare since 2021, with a filter to show only lower-emissions alternatives. Skyscanner also offers a similar filter. However, neither lets you actually purchase SAF. Price is also part of BookBetter’s ranking algorithm, so lower-emission options don’t necessarily mean choosing the most expensive flight.

“BookBetter ranks flights by combining emissions and price in a single algorithm, so the option that rises to the top is a genuinely better value in every sense,” Lammertyn explained. In practice, that means the platform tends to favor routes and flight options that are already cheaper, with a direct flight on a newer aircraft in economy (which also happens to be the cleaner option) usually costing less than a connection in business class.

But Lammertyn is clear on the fact that none of this adds up to a perfect solution.

“We do not want to call it fully sustainable, since even on 100 percent SAF, a flight would still have a negative climate effect of around 20 percent of the fossil CO2 it emits today,” he said, pointing to non-CO2 warming effects as an additional factor they cannot control. If you really want the most sustainable travel choice, his advice is to take a train. (BookBetter has a rail tab on its site to help you with that, too.) But when you have to fly, make it count.

According to Lammertyn, more than 30,000 people have tested BookBetter to date, including travelers who don’t necessarily consider sustainability their primary concern.

“The traveler the industry keeps calling niche, the one who wants to go far, go well, and leave the smallest mark possible, turns out to be far more common than anyone admitted,” he said. “You do not have to stop exploring the world. You just deserve a platform that helps you do it better.”

title: Brazil's Petrobras uses Cardano to track sustainable aviation fuel, renewable diesel
description:
Brazilian state-controlled oil company Petrobras has developed two blockchain applications using Cardano to track sustainability data for sustainable aviation fuel (SAF) and its Diesel R renewable fuel.
Source: Cardano Foundation The second application creates digital checkpoints to track the production, transportation and use of Diesel R, Petrobras’ renewable diesel fuel.
The Cardano Foundation said the data could support Scope 3 reporting, which covers indirect emissions across a company’s value chain.
The Cardano Foundation did not disclose fuel volumes covered by the applications or a timeline for broader deployment.
Blockchain finds use in sustainable aviation fuel tracking Shell has also used blockchain to track environmental attributes associated with sustainable aviation fuel through Avelia, a Book-and-Claim platform launched in 2022 that uses blockchain to track claims and prevent double counting.
text:
Brazilian state-controlled oil company Petrobras has developed two blockchain applications using Cardano to track sustainability data for sustainable aviation fuel (SAF) and its Diesel R renewable fuel.

According to a Wednesday announcement from the Cardano Foundation, the first application, developed with PUC-Rio’s Ledger Labs, tokenizes environmental attributes associated with SAF into digital tokens designed to prevent the same claim from being used more than once.

The application uses a Book-and-Claim model, which allows the environmental benefit to be separated from the physical fuel and assigned to an airline, company or passenger even if the SAF is used elsewhere.

The tokens, known as CS-SAF, contain metadata aligned with the Carbon Offsetting and Reduction Scheme for International Aviation (CORSIA). Passengers can also claim CS-SAF tokens through an application and receive a certificate tied to their journey and associated environmental claim.

Source: Cardano Foundation

The second application creates digital checkpoints to track the production, transportation and use of Diesel R, Petrobras’ renewable diesel fuel. The Cardano Foundation said the data could support Scope 3 reporting, which covers indirect emissions across a company’s value chain.

The projects are part of an ongoing research and development collaboration that began in 2023 with blockchain education for Petrobras employees and expanded in 2025 to energy-sector research with PUC-Rio’s Ledger Labs. The Cardano Foundation did not disclose fuel volumes covered by the applications or a timeline for broader deployment.

Blockchain finds use in sustainable aviation fuel tracking

Shell has also used blockchain to track environmental attributes associated with sustainable aviation fuel through Avelia, a Book-and-Claim platform launched in 2022 that uses blockchain to track claims and prevent double counting.

In a September update, Shell said Avelia had contributed to more than 84 million gallons of SAF entering the global fuel network since its launch in 2022, resulting in more than 780,000 tonnes of CO₂e abatement through June 2026.

More recently, Australia’s Viva Energy signed an agreement with NoviqTech in January to research digital Book-and-Claim systems for sustainable aviation fuel, including how blockchain could support emissions reporting and track environmental claims.

title: Sustainable Fuels - DHL - United States of America
description:
At DHL, we have expanded our Sustainable Aviation Fuel (SAF) supply network globally.
Alternative marine fuels may lower well-to-wake GHG emissions relative to petroleum-based marine fuels, depending on the production pathway and engine technology.
LNG dominates this transition, followed by methanol, with ammonia and hydrogen fuels still at an early stage of adoption.
Governments are actively supporting the growth of sustainable fuels through blending mandates, incentives, and regulatory frameworks and major energy companies such as Neste are accelerating investments in low-carbon fuels.
These fuels can reduce lifecycle emissions by up to roughly 75% compared to fossil fuels.
text:
SAF is currently the principal drop-in alternative to conventional jet fuel for reducing lifecycle GHG emissions from long-distance air freight without replacing existing aircraft and fuel infrastructure. Hydrogen and battery solutions remain in early stages, making full electrification not yet viable. As a result, SAF serves as the key commercial pathway for decarbonizing aviation.

Certain SAF pathways can deliver lifecycle GHG-emissions reductions of around 80% compared with conventional aviation fuel, although actual performance varies by feedstock, production pathway, and accounting methodology. Despite this potential, supply remains extremely limited, accounting for only a small share of global aviation fuel, highlighting the urgent need to scale production through greater investment and demand.

In 2025, SAF output reached approximately 2.4 billion liters (1.9 million metric tons), nearly double the 1 million metric tons produced in 2024 – yet it still accounts for only around 0.6% of total jet fuel consumption. SAF production growth is expected to decelerate in 2026 due to high price premiums, policy gaps as well as limited market maturity, underscoring the continued gap between supply and demand.

Availability and high cost remain barriers to widespread adoption. SAFs are derived from renewable sources such as biomass, animal fats, oils, and alcohol, which can be blended with conventional kerosene. Industry initiatives have brought together aviation stakeholders to support SAF market development and the reduction of lifecycle GHG emissions from aviation.

At DHL, we have expanded our Sustainable Aviation Fuel (SAF) supply network globally. By 2025, we used approximately 185 metric kilotons of SAF, achieving a SAF blend of roughly 10% across our air operations. This represents one of the highest SAF utilization shares among global airlines, reflecting DHL's commitment to accelerating the transition toward more sustainable air transport. In May 2026, we added the first SAF production facility in the Middle East to our global network, signing an agreement with SAF One to secure 25,000 metric tons annually for 10 years from the company’s Bahrain plant.

Looking further ahead, hydrogen-derived e-fuels and other synthetic aviation fuels remain promising long-term solutions. Startups like H2FLY and ZeroAvia are working on promising concepts, but experts do not expect commercial application of sub-regional and regional hydrogen fuel cell aircraft before 2030. However, DHL experts view the scaling of SAF from advanced feedstocks such as novel vegetable oils, agricultural residues, and municipal solid waste as the more immediate priority.

International maritime transportation, including vessels ranging from small recreational boats to massive, ocean-going container ships, accounts for roughly 2 to 3% of global greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions, with total emissions estimated at 900 to 1,000 million metric tons of CO₂e annually.

More than 80% of global traded goods are transported by cargo ships, 95% of which rely on heavy fuel oil (HFO) for propulsion, a residual fuel produced from petroleum refining, which emits relatively large amounts of GHG when combusted.

Alternative marine fuels may lower well-to-wake GHG emissions relative to petroleum-based marine fuels, depending on the production pathway and engine technology. Some alternatives can also reduce sulfur oxides and certain local air pollutants at the point of use, although pollutant profiles vary by fuel and combustion system.

A wide range of SMFs are being explored, each with distinct characteristics.

Fossil LNG is currently the most widely adopted alternative marine fuel, but its well-to-wake GHG performance relative to fuel oil depends on upstream methane emissions and methane slip from the engine; it therefore remains a fossil-based option.

LPG provides reduced emissions and benefits from established infrastructure, making it a practical near-term option, however its long-term viability is challenged by its fossil origins and strict safety hazards.

Methanol is a versatile and scalable fuel with simpler handling and growing adoption potential, although supply and cost remain challenges.

Biofuels provide a near-term, drop-in solution compatible with existing engines, though scalability is constrained by feedstock availability and sustainability considerations.

Ammonia contains no carbon and therefore produces no CO₂ at the point of use, but its well-to-wake GHG performance depends on how it is produced and managed; storage, toxicity, nitrous oxide emissions, safety, and infrastructure remain challenges.

Electric propulsion enables highly efficient, low-emission operations for short-range vessels but is limited by battery energy density and operational range.

Hydrogen fuel cells produce no CO₂ at the point of use, although lifecycle GHG emissions depend on hydrogen production and supply. Storage volume, infrastructure, safety, and technology maturity remain barriers to maritime deployment.

Nuclear propulsion offers high energy density and produces no direct combustion-related GHG emissions during operation, but lifecycle impacts, radioactive waste, security, regulatory, safety, and public-acceptance issues remain significant.

Taken together, these tradeoffs indicate that the maritime sector will likely follow a multi-fuel transition pathway depending on vessel types, routes, and infrastructure readiness.

Despite low fuel penetration, fleet transition is accelerating rapidly, reflecting a growing readiness to adopt sustainable fuels. In 2025, ship owners increasingly ordered alternative-fuel-capable vessels across leisure and merchant ships. Vessel fuel capabilities are diversified across LNG, methanol, ammonia, and hydrogen-based fuel. LNG dominates this transition, followed by methanol, with ammonia and hydrogen fuels still at an early stage of adoption.

The GHG intensity of maritime transport varies by vessel efficiency, utilization, route, fuel pathway, and the lifecycle boundary applied.

The future of marine fuels is not a single-fuel shift but a gradual transition to a diversified fuel mix, with retrofitting of existing fleets and scaling of alternative fuel supply as the key enablers of decarbonization.

Although electric vehicles (EVs) are rapidly becoming mainstream for short to medium distance transport, especially in light-duty and urban use, electrification remains challenging for long-haul, heavy-duty transport due to limited range, long charging times, and a shortage of suitable high-capacity truck models. This means the industry continues to rely on combustion engines running on fossil fuels.

Sustainable fuels represent a key near-term solution for decarbonization in road transportation, playing a complementary role to electrification, particularly for segments that are difficult to electrify. Biofuels are currently the most practical option because they can be blended with conventional diesel. The IEA forecasts that the share of biofuels in road transportation will rise from 5% in 2022 to 10% in 2030.

This momentum is reinforced by policy and a strong shift by traditional fuel producers toward biofuels and synthetic fuels. Governments are actively supporting the growth of sustainable fuels through blending mandates, incentives, and regulatory frameworks and major energy companies such as Neste are accelerating investments in low-carbon fuels. The company’s capacity is expected to reach roughly 6.8 million metric tons annually by 2027.

The two primary truck biofuels in use are biodiesel (FAME) and hydrotreated vegetable oil (HVO). Biodiesel is derived from vegetable oils or waste fats (for example, recycled fats from the catering industry) and can be blended with conventional diesel (typically up to 7% in many regions such as the EU). HVO is vegetable oil that has been treated with hydrogen, offering similar properties to fossil diesel that allow higher blend levels or even 100% substitution.

E-fuels are another emerging class of sustainable fuels, produced using captured CO₂ and green hydrogen from water split by low-carbon electricity sources including wind and solar. These fuels can reduce lifecycle emissions by up to roughly 75% compared to fossil fuels. Adoption remains limited due to high production costs and early-stage commercialization, with large-scale deployment dependent on further technological and policy support.

Warehouses are among the most energy-intensive building types, with material handling, heating, and hot water accounting for a considerable share of total energy demand. Electrification is the default decarbonization pathway, but it has real limits. Alternative fuels may address some warehouse energy uses that are not readily electrified and may reduce relevant Scope 1 emissions, depending on the fuel pathway. Renewable electricity is an energy source rather than a fuel and primarily affects market- or location-based Scope 2 reporting.

Today, a significant share of material handling equipment (MHE) in modern warehouses, such as forklifts and pallet movers, is already electrified and powered by batteries. Electrified material-handling equipment produces no direct exhaust emissions at the point of use; associated Scope 2 and lifecycle GHG emissions depend on the electricity supply and accounting method.

However, battery-powered systems still present operational challenges in high-throughput environments, including charging downtime, battery swapping requirements, and space constraints for charging infrastructure.

Hydrogen fuel cell technology is gaining traction for MHE, particularly in large-scale, high-intensity warehouse operations. Fuel cell-powered forklifts offer continuous operation without battery degradation, significantly reducing downtime. Refueling takes approximately 2 to 3 minutes, compared to several hours required for battery charging, while fuel-cell operation produces no direct CO₂ or combustion-related air-pollutant emissions at the point of use, while lifecycle GHG emissions depend on hydrogen production and supply.

This makes hydrogen particularly suitable for multi-shift, high-utilization environments where operational efficiency and uptime are critical. Leading companies such as Amazon and BMW have already deployed hydrogen fuel cell forklifts at scale in their distribution and manufacturing facilities.

Beyond material handling, building heating and hot water present a different decarbonization hurdle. Electrification of these thermal loads can be challenging at scale, particularly in colder climates or large industrial facilities. In this context, Biomethane upgraded to the applicable gas-grid specification can be used in many existing natural-gas boilers and CHP systems. Its lifecycle GHG performance depends on feedstock, methane leakage, processing, transport, avoided-emissions assumptions, and the accounting method applied.

RNG is chemically identical to fossil natural gas and can be used directly in existing infrastructure, including boilers and combined heat and power (CHP) systems, without requiring major retrofits. Produced from organic waste streams such as agricultural residues, landfill gas, and wastewater, RNG supports circular economy principles while enabling immediate emissions reduction in heating applications.

Sustainable fuels for warehouse operations allow logistics providers to take a more holistic approach to decarbonizing supply chains – extending efforts beyond transport. This supports compliance with emerging regulatory frameworks and aligns with growing customer demand for end-to-end low-carbon logistics solutions.

text:
Delta Air Lines joined partners across Georgia to launch the Georgia Sustainable Aviation Fuel (SAF) Coalition, a new statewide effort established by the Metro Atlanta Chamber and founding members Delta, the Georgia Forestry Association and Georgia Farm Bureau. The coalition aims to advance SAF production and drive economic investment across Georgia. SAF is an alternative jet fuel made from renewable feedstocks that can significantly reduce lifecycle carbon emissions compared to conventional jet fuel.

During an event at the Delta Flight Museum, elected officials, industry leaders and coalition partners gathered to highlight Georgia's opportunity to become a leader in sustainable aviation fuel production. Speakers included Georgia House Speaker Jon Burns, Georgia Agriculture Commissioner Tyler Harper, Metro Atlanta Chamber President and CEO Katie Kirkpatrick and Delta President Peter Carter.

"Georgia is well positioned to become a national leader in SAF," said Peter Carter, President of Delta Air Lines. "The Georgia SAF Coalition unites organizations committed to advancing that opportunity. Together, we can power the growth of a SAF industry that strengthens Georgia’s economy, supports innovation and creates lasting benefits for communities across the state.”

The coalition builds on momentum created by this year's Keep Georgia Forested Act, legislation that encourages investment in forestry manufacturing and creates new opportunities to convert Georgia-grown agricultural and forestry feedstocks into products such as sustainable aviation fuel.

Priorities include strengthening public-private partnerships, supporting research and commercialization, attracting investment, advancing policies that support industry growth and connecting Georgia's existing strengths to emerging opportunities.

As home to Delta's global headquarters and the world's busiest airport, Georgia is already helping shape the future of aviation. Combined with the nation's largest forestry resource base, strong agricultural production, leading research institutions and a robust logistics network, the state is uniquely positioned to build a sustainable aviation fuel ecosystem that supports farmers, foresters and local communities while creating new economic opportunities across Georgia.

SAF is widely viewed as one of the most promising tools available today to reduce lifecycle carbon emissions from air travel, and Georgia has the feedstock resources, research capabilities and business leadership needed to help scale the industry.

title: CodeWatch: Big wins for off-site construction and embodied carbon reduction - SmartBrief
description:
Modular and off-site construction finally has a consistent code framework in the 2027 I-Codes, and a new research report makes the case that structural codes are the next frontier for embodied carbon reduction.
Those threads run alongside updates to head protection standards, a suite of ASTM worker safety tools and a milestone for alternative energy.

Some proposals, if adopted, could reduce a structure’s embodied carbon by as much as 12% against current code baselines.
However, because Version 3 tightens the data consistency requirements for upstream cement and aggregate suppliers, the carbon scores of some standard concrete mixes may shift slightly.
text:
Building codes are notoriously slow to absorb new construction methods, but two developments this month suggest the gap is narrowing on multiple fronts. Modular and off-site construction finally has a consistent code framework in the 2027 I-Codes, and a new research report makes the case that structural codes are the next frontier for embodied carbon reduction. Those threads run alongside updates to head protection standards, a suite of ASTM worker safety tools and a milestone for alternative energy.

A win for off-site construction

One persistent friction point for modular and panelized construction has been the absence of a uniform approval framework across jurisdictions. A project manufactured in one state and installed in another could face entirely different review processes at each end. The 2027 I-Codes could change that.

The new editions of the International Code Council’s International Building Code and International Residential Code incorporate the ICC/MBI 1200 series (standards 1200, 1205, and 1210), which together establish a common framework for how off-site building components are reviewed and approved. Seven states have already adopted the ICC/MBI standards, with Maine and New Hampshire among the most recent. The standards have also been incorporated into the Department of War’s Uniform Facilities Criteria for military construction, reflecting the department’s interest in scaling off-site methods for defense projects.

Ryan Colker, ICC’s executive director of energy, resilience and innovation, said the incorporation is meant to reduce barriers that have historically slowed projects even when the construction method itself was well-suited to the task. That means a single compliance path, rather than jurisdiction-by-jurisdiction negotiation, becomes available wherever the 2027 I-Codes are adopted.

Structural codes enter the embodied carbon conversation

A report from the first phase of the Code Updates for Reduction of Embodied Carbon project, known as CURE, offers the most systematic effort to date to connect structural building codes to carbon outcomes. The work was led by researchers at the University of Colorado Boulder and funded by the Pankow Foundation, along with the ACI Foundation (a non-profit subsidiary of the American Concrete Institute), the American Institute of Steel Construction, the American Society of Civil Engineers’ Structural Engineering Institute, the Magnusson Klemencic Associates Foundation, and the National Council of Structural Engineers Association Foundation.

The Phase 1 report identifies 11 priority code changes for the committees that govern ACI 318 (structural concrete), AISC 360 (structural steel) and ASCE 7 (design loads). The proposed changes reduce embodied carbon either by enabling smaller required section sizes or by allowing lower design-strength concrete, which reduces the carbon intensity of the mix. Some proposals, if adopted, could reduce a structure’s embodied carbon by as much as 12% against current code baselines. The authors note that reductions of even 1 to 3% are meaningful given the scale of the building industry’s total output.

The report frames structural engineers, rather than architects or owners, as the profession with the most direct leverage over embodied carbon in a building’s structure. Each proposal is presented with an estimated impact and a description of the research needed to support a formal code change proposal, and the authors describe the changes as achievable in the near term with targeted, funded work.

New concrete PCR changes how carbon gets counted

Tying directly to the CURE project’s ambitions is a change in how the carbon performance of concrete gets measured and reported. The National Ready Mixed Concrete Association, through NSF International, published NSF 1112-26 — Version 3 of the Product Category Rule for concrete environmental product declarations. The update, valid through April 30, 2031, is the result of two years of work involving producers, government agencies, trade associations and life cycle analysis experts.

An EPD functions roughly like a nutritional label for a concrete mix’s environmental footprint. What controls how that label is produced is the PCR, and the update to Version 3 changes several of the accounting rules. The new version expands scope and definitions, incorporates newer supplementary cementitious material and cement technologies, improves the treatment of portable batch plants and mobile volumetric mixers, which previously lacked a clear calculation path, and tightens data quality requirements.

Under federal and state Buy Clean laws, bids on public infrastructure projects require an EPD produced under the current valid PCR. As EPDs generated under the prior Version 2.3 expire, contractors will need to request updated Version 3-compliant EPDs from their ready-mix suppliers. NRMCA’s Tiffany Reed-Villarreal framed the revision as essential infrastructure for the industry’s credibility on carbon. Without consistent accounting rules across producers, the numbers reported on EPDs aren’t reliably comparable.

However, because Version 3 tightens the data consistency requirements for upstream cement and aggregate suppliers, the carbon scores of some standard concrete mixes may shift slightly. Not because the mix changed, but because the accounting rules did.

Head protection standard revised for evolving jobsite risks

The International Safety Equipment Association published a revised American National Standard for Industrial Head Protection, ANSI/ISEA Z89.1-2026, updating a standard that governs how hard hats and safety helmets are classified, tested, and marked.

The revision does not render existing compliant equipment obsolete. It retains the established Type and Class designations for impact, penetration, and electrical protection. What it adds is a new optional “+” designation that identifies head protection tested beyond the base standard for chin strap retention, helmet retention under movement, and multi-point impact coverage on the front, rear, and sides. The “+” marking also includes verified performance for reverse wearing, a real-world practice common in trades work that previous editions didn’t explicitly address.

ISEA also updated the visibility marking system. What was previously labeled “High Visibility (HV)” becomes “Enhanced Visibility (EV)” to clarify that head protection is evaluated under different criteria than high-visibility apparel governed by ANSI/ISEA 107. The change addresses a persistent source of confusion among safety professionals selecting equipment across both product categories.

ISEA CEO Cam Mackey described the update as more than a routine revision, citing nearly 700 worker fatalities attributed to head injuries over the past year. The revision reflects pressure from major employers who have moved beyond minimum requirements and needed a standardized framework to describe and evaluate the enhanced protection they’re already mandating on their sites.

A suite for serious injury prevention

ASTM’s occupational health and safety committee (E34) has updated a suite of three related standards that together create a framework for moving beyond incident counting toward actual risk reduction.

E2920 establishes how workplace injuries and illnesses are recorded and categorized by severity across four levels, from fatal and serious injury events down to minor incidents and near misses. Its companion, E3519, extends the same recording framework to non-injury events — fires, environmental releases, and business interruptions — that carry the same lethal potential without always producing a recordable injury. Both standards address what safety professionals have long recognized as a gap in the mandatory OSHA reporting system: that it tracks whether incidents occurred and were recorded, but not how close a near miss came to causing a fatality.

E3529 is the forward-looking piece of the suite. It provides a risk identification and prioritization framework specifically designed for serious injury and fatality hazards, allowing organizations to install safeguards before an incident happens rather than after.

A fourth standard, WK92350, is in development and would create a framework for assessing worker engagement in safety programs from the shop floor to the executive level. ASTM member Marty Stern of Colgate-Palmolive framed the goal as shifting safety culture from top-down compliance toward a system that actively draws on the knowledge of workers who encounter hazards directly.

Alternative energy standards mark a milestone

In May 2026, utility-scale solar plants in the US generated more electricity than coal-fired plants for the first time — 12.8% of national output versus coal’s 12.2%. ASTM’s Standardization News covers how the organization’s committees are building the standards infrastructure that underlies the transition.

On the solar side, ASTM’s E44 committee maintains standards for testing material absorptance, reflectance, and transmittance (E903), and for sampling retired PV modules to determine toxicity before disposal (E3325) — an increasingly active issue as the earliest large-scale solar installations approach end of life. On wind, the D02 committee’s lubricant standards, including D1092 and D1831, govern the greases that must perform reliably in wind turbine gearboxes across temperature ranges from -20° to 120°F. On hydrogen, the D03 committee’s nine active standards address sampling and purity testing for hydrogen fuel, including methods for detecting trace gaseous contaminants via FTIR spectroscopy.

For nuclear, the C26 committee revised standard C1934 in 2025 to address uranium hexafluoride enriched at 5 to 8 percent 235U and published new standard C1962 covering 8 to 20 percent enrichment levels — specifications that support advanced reactor designs requiring higher-enriched fuel for longer operational cycles. The DOE announced in July that a fourth authorized nuclear reactor design in the U.S. had reached criticality, driven in part by the 2025 executive order aimed at reinvigorating the domestic nuclear industrial base.

Quantum sensors sharpen nuclear material accounting

Researchers using quantum sensors developed at the National Institute of Standards and Technology have measured X-ray emissions from uranium, plutonium, and neptunium with precision that reduces previous measurement uncertainty by factors of three to eight. The sensors operate at temperatures just above absolute zero, where even the energy of a single incoming photon produces a detectable resistance change in a superconducting film.

The practical application is nuclear safeguards. Verifying enrichment levels and accounting for nuclear material at power plants and weapons facilities requires distinguishing X-ray emissions from overlapping gamma-ray signals, a historically difficult measurement problem. NIST physicist Jonathan Dean said the new measurements directly support international safeguards work by enabling more precise material accounting. NIST has already installed TES detectors at three DOE national laboratories, with additional deployments at research facilities including Argonne, Brookhaven, SLAC and CERN.

title: Cardano Foundation Advances Renewable Fuel Traceability
description:
As part of an ongoing R&D collaboration, the teams have delivered two blockchain applications focused on sustainable aviation fuel (SAF) and Diesel R, Petrobras’ brand of renewable fuel.
These initiatives address different parts of the renewable fuel lifecycle.
Making sustainable aviation fuel claims traceable The SAF R&D project brings together Petrobras, PUC-Rio through its blockchain center Ledger Labs, and the Cardano Foundation.
Extending traceability across renewable diesel A second Petrobras project, developed with PUC-Rio, applies Cardano to Diesel R, Petrobras’ brand of renewable diesel.
“The energy transition will depend as much on trust as it does on new fuels,” said Rafael Fraga, LATAM Business Development Lead at the Cardano Foundation.
text:
Zug, Switzerland, Rio de Janeiro, Brazil, 30 September 2026 – The Cardano Foundation, the independent, Swiss-based not-for-profit organization dedicated to advancing Cardano as public digital infrastructure, today announced two new initiatives with Petrobras, Brazil’s state-controlled energy firm and one of Latin America’s most valuable companies. As part of an ongoing R&D collaboration, the teams have delivered two blockchain applications focused on sustainable aviation fuel (SAF) and Diesel R, Petrobras’ brand of renewable fuel.

Brazil’s oil and gas market is projected to reach USD 28.82 billion by 2031, underscoring the scale of the sector in which these initiatives are being developed. Against that backdrop, both projects focus on a specific challenge: making environmental claims and fuel lifecycle data easier to trace and verify.

These initiatives address different parts of the renewable fuel lifecycle. For SAF, Cardano connects a physical fuel certificate to a digital record of the associated environmental gains, creating a clear trail from the original certificate through to the final claim. For renewable diesel, the technology links information across production, transportation and use, improving visibility over the fuel journey and the emissions-related data associated with it.

Making sustainable aviation fuel claims traceable

The SAF R&D project brings together Petrobras, PUC-Rio through its blockchain center Ledger Labs, and the Cardano Foundation. Sustainable aviation fuel is a lower-carbon alternative to conventional jet fuel that can be used within existing aviation infrastructure. As adoption grows, airlines and passengers also need credible ways to verify the environmental benefit associated with its use.

The project uses a Book-and-Claim model, which separates that environmental benefit from the physical fuel itself. This allows the benefit to be assigned to an airline, company or passenger even when the SAF is produced or used elsewhere. Cardano provides the traceable record behind the process, showing where the benefit originated, who it was assigned to and that it has only been claimed once.

The application also extends to individual passengers. Travelers can enter their departure and destination airports, calculate the corresponding CS-SAF amount – the digital token used to represent the SAF environmental benefit – and receive a certificate recording their route, distance traveled and allocation. This links the passenger’s claim back to the original SAF certificate.

Extending traceability across renewable diesel

A second Petrobras project, developed with PUC-Rio, applies Cardano to Diesel R, Petrobras’ brand of renewable diesel. The proposed model creates digital checkpoints across production, transportation and use, converting information from each stage into a continuous record of the fuel’s lifecycle.

This is particularly relevant for reporting of Scope 3 greenhouse-gas emissions, which covers indirect emissions generated across a company’s wider value chain and often relies on data spread across suppliers, logistics providers and other external systems. By connecting those record the model can create a clearer supply-chain history and strengthen the traceability and auditability of information used in emissions accounting.

“The energy transition will depend as much on trust as it does on new fuels,” said Rafael Fraga, LATAM Business Development Lead at the Cardano Foundation. “As value chains become more complex, proving where environmental data comes from, how it moves and who can rely on it becomes critical. Public blockchain gives us the opportunity to make that trust part of the system by design, providing industries with a shared, verifiable foundation for the next generation of energy markets.”

The two projects apply the same underlying principle to different parts of the energy transition: creating a reliable digital trail for information that today often sits across fragmented systems, organizations and supply chains.

The work adds to the Cardano Foundation’s growing portfolio of real-world blockchain applications in Brazil, demonstrating how public digital infrastructure can support industries where provenance, transparency and auditability are increasingly important.
