Petrobras, Brazil’s state-controlled energy company, is testing the Cardano blockchain to track claims about lower-carbon fuel, in two research projects announced Wednesday by the Cardano Foundation shared with CoinDesk.

One covers sustainable aviation fuel, a lower-carbon alternative to conventional jet fuel that can be used in existing aircraft and airports. The other covers Diesel R, Petrobras’ diesel made partly from renewable materials such as vegetable oils or animal fats.

“Brazil has been one of the most consistent adopters of Cardano, from SERPRO in government to SENAI in industry. It's great to see Petrobras, one of the largest firms in the region, continue to see value in on-chain provenance and traceability,” Frederik Gregaard, chief executive of the Cardano Foundation, told CoinDesk.

“Institutional interest in Cardano keeps growing, especially with x402 arriving on Cardano and Fireblocks adding support for Cardano Native Tokens. It's never been a better time for enterprises to consider what this technology offers,” Gregaard added.

The aviation project tackles a problem with how green fuel is sold. Under a model known as book-and-claim, an airline can pay for the environmental benefit of sustainable fuel even if the fuel itself is used elsewhere.

That arrangement needs a record of who owns the benefit and when it has been claimed, so two companies cannot count the same emissions reduction.

The application uses Cardano to record where each benefit originated, who received it and when it was claimed, helping prevent it from being counted twice.

In the real world, a passenger can enter their departure and destination airports, calculate the corresponding fuel benefit and receive a certificate linking their allocation back to the original fuel certificate.

On the other hand, the diesel project would record information at each stage of production, transportation and use, joining those records into a history of the fuel’s journey.

That could help companies report Scope 3 emissions, the indirect emissions across their suppliers and customers, where the information needed often sits with other businesses.

Both projects remain research work. The diesel model is described as proposed, and the announcement disclosed neither fuel volumes covered nor a timeline for wider use.

Cardano also joined x402 this month, a payment standard that lets apps and AI agents pay for data or computing services as they request them. Its initial payment-processing software had been tested on Cardano’s pre-production network, with commercial use on the live blockchain still to be demonstrated.

text:
The Sustainable Aviation Buyers Alliance (SABA) on Sept. 22 announced commitments from members to purchase sustainable aviation fuel certificates (SAFc) associated with Infinium Energy's Project Atlas, an eSAF facility expected to produce approximately 100,000 metric tons of SAF annually, providing the long-term structured contracts that are catalytic to securing project financing.

The groundbreaking results of SABA's latest procurement were supported by leading member organizations, including AVEVA, Bain & Company, Google, McKinsey, and others, and mark an important addition to SABA's market model. Through exclusive focus on supporting projects toward final investment decision, this procurement represents a first-ever application of SABA's approach to drive new production of highly scalable, high-integrity SAF. Infinium submitted its winning proposal jointly with American Airlines, which will take physical delivery of the fuel and oversee fuel logistics. Contracted volumes under these agreements are expected to support greenhouse gas abatement of over 212,000 mtCO2e, equivalent to the emissions of over 3,500 JFK to LAX commercial flights.

"Reducing emissions from business travel is an important part of our sustainability efforts," said Isabelle Schuhmann, global director of environmental sustainability at McKinsey. "By supporting next-generation sustainable aviation fuel, this purchase helps advance a promising solution for decarbonizing aviation at scale, while enabling the travel that is essential to serving our clients."

Aviation currently accounts for approximately 2-3% of global greenhouse gas emissions, yet SAF supply remains limited and at a significant premium to conventional jet fuel. Infinium, which was selected through SABA's procurement process earlier this year, produces ultra-low carbon eSAF at commercial scale using waste CO₂ and renewable energy, converting captured carbon into drop-in aviation fuel compatible with existing aircraft and infrastructure.

"We're proud to partner with SABA members including AVEVA, Bain & Company, Google, McKinsey, and others, as well as American Airlines to bring Infinium Energy's next world scale eSAF facility to life," said Robert Schuetzle, CEO at Infinium. "Their commitment reflects a shared conviction that decarbonizing aviation requires real investment in next-generation supply."

"The companies purchasing SAF certificates through this agreement are demonstrating the leadership needed to help scale a critical solution for aviation," said American's Chief Sustainability Officer Jill Blickstein. "Their commitments broaden participation in the SAF market, support investment in new production and show how customers can work alongside airlines and fuel producers to advance aviation decarbonization."

SABA procurements use a book and claim model that allows corporate customers to invest in SAF and claim the associated environmental benefits, even when the fuel does not flow directly into the planes their employees or freight fly on. Participating companies purchase SAFc, while the corresponding fuel is delivered to an aircraft operator. American Airlines will serve as the physical offtaker for the SAF purchased through this deal and facilitate the allocation of the associated Scope 3 emission reductions to SABA's participating members.

"Next-generation sustainable aviation fuels have tremendous potential to transform aviation," said Sam Israelit, Chief Sustainability Officer at Bain & Company. "High-integrity market mechanisms can help translate corporate demand into the long-term investment signals needed to bring these technologies to commercial scale."

While the SAF market is growing rapidly, more investment is needed, especially for the next generation technologies the aviation sector requires to meet its long-term decarbonization goals. SABA helps accelerate future supply by aggregating SAF demand from corporate buyers and channeling it into offtake agreements with SAFc suppliers who meet rigorous sustainability criteria. SABA's next generation SAF procurement was specifically designed to drive investment into the innovative new technologies needed to bring scalable supply to the market in the years to come.

"Long-term, bankable offtake is often the missing puzzle piece that keeps new SAF plants from getting financed and built," said Kim Carnahan, GMA CEO and Head of SABA Secretariat. "We're thrilled to be working with our SABA members, Infinium, and American Airlines to fill this need and help get more ultra-low carbon aviation fuel to the market."

"We already know innovation can take us much further, faster, but only if we create the conditions for it to scale," said Jon Creyts, CEO of RMI. "Novel technologies are critical to meeting future demand for sustainable aviation fuel, but they will not be operational in time without investments made today. This procurement demonstrates how aggregated, long-term demand can help take promising eSAF projects from idea to reality."

To date, SABA has aggregated $500 million in demand for SAFc from over 35 member companies, driving needed investment toward sustainable aviation fuels. SABA's procurements are supported by robust market infrastructure, including the SAFc Registry, SAFc Accounting and Reporting Guidance, and SABA's Sustainability Framework. Combined, these tools ensure high-integrity transactions across the market. Recent guidance from standard setting organizations, including the Science-based Targets initiative, has recognized environmental attribute certificates from book and claim systems, like SAFc, as a legitimate tool for decarbonizing hard-to-abate value chain emissions.

With the binding, multi-year offtake agreements from SABA customers in hand, Infinium is well positioned to advance to final investment decision and secure financing to build the facility. In addition to serving voluntary customers, Infinium also plans to sell RFNBO compliant eSAF from the facility into European regulatory markets.

"eFuels represent one of the most sustainable pathways to help decarbonize aviation — but they are more expensive to produce," said Fred Krupp, president of Environmental Defense Fund. "Deals like this one prove that high-integrity e-SAF is investable today, not just in theory. The next test is turning early demand signals like SABA's into the long-term policy and financing conditions that will enable e-SAF suppliers to scale beyond a single project."

Plans for SABA's next procurement are already underway, offering future opportunities for companies to purchase and apply SAFc to their climate targets.

description:

The X1 is an airplane built by a company called Heart Aerospace to test its plans for battery-powered flight.

text:
Plattsburgh, New York —(Map)

On August 12, a 30-seat airplane weighing 25,000 pounds (11,340 kilograms) took off from an airport in New York state. That may sound fairly ordinary, but there was something that made this plane unusual: it was the world’s largest electric plane.

The X1 is an airplane built by a company called Heart Aerospace to test its plans for battery-powered flight. The plane is 106 feet (32 meters) from wingtip to wingtip, and 76 feet (23 meters) long. It weighs about as much as a city bus, and it may help point to the future of air travel.

For its August flight, the pilot raced the X1 down the runway and took off. Because it was a test flight, there were no passengers. The 30-seat aircraft climbed to 1,100 feet (335 meters) and flew for 27 minutes. The electricity needed for the entire flight cost about $5.

That’s a big deal. Airlines are expected to spend about $350 billion on jet fuel in 2026 alone. Since the US-Iran war began in February, jet fuel costs have climbed from $2.39 a gallon to $3.50 a gallon ($0.63 a liter to $0.92 a liter). So a $5 flight sounds like a bargain.

Heart believes that the X1, and the planes that follow it, could bring big changes for airlines. Currently, transportation by air is responsible for about 2.5% of the world’s greenhouse gas pollution. Planes that run on electricity could help reduce these emissions.

But electric planes face a big challenge: their weight. Batteries are heavy. Adding enough batteries to go long distances limits how many passengers or how much cargo a plane can carry.

The X1 can only fly about 125 miles (200 kilometers) at a time. And planes always have to have extra fuel for emergencies. So for now, most battery-powered aircraft are air taxis, which only travel short distances.

Heart has a different idea in mind. It plans to build a “hybrid” airplane called the ES-30. Like a hybrid car, this plane would fly on electricity part of the time, and run on jet fuel the rest of the time. This would expand the ES-30’s range to about 500 miles (800 kilometers). Heart believes its hybrid design would reduce the plane’s costs (flying it and keeping it in good shape) by over 40%.

With its longer range, the hybrid ES-30 is expected to be able to work well for “regional” air travel, like the short flights commonly made between cities in the US or in Europe.

Heart isn’t the only company working on battery-powered and hybrid planes. But the plans for the ES-30 have gotten a lot of attention. Several airlines have shown interest in the ES-30. United Airlines has agreed to buy 100 of the planes.

But it will be some time before that happens. For Heart, the next step is to build the X2. That’s the plane Heart will use to test its hybrid system. If all goes well, Heart hopes the ES-30 will begin carrying passengers for airlines by 2031.

text:
The Civil Aviation Authority of Vietnam (CAAV) is coordinating efforts to develop a roadmap for the adoption of Sustainable Aviation Fuel (SAF), while completing regulations on greenhouse gas emissions reduction in civil aviation, according to a report submitted to the Ministry of Construction.

The CAAV noted that the roadmap aims to prevent market and airline "shocks" during the transition to sustainable fuels.

On the regulatory front, the CAAV is drafting a circular outlining regulations on greenhouse gas emissions mitigation and environmental protection in civil aviation operations to seek feedback from relevant ministries and agencies. These regulations align with International Civil Aviation Organization (ICAO) standards and support Vietnam’s national commitment to achieving net-zero emissions by 2050.

In production, domestic enterprises have begun researching technologies and feedstocks for SAF processing. Petrovietnam has tasked BSR (Binh Son Refining and Petrochemical) and PVOIL with executing relevant initiatives. Specifically, BSR is exploring investment opportunities in SAF production using Hydroprocessed Esters and Fatty Acids (HEFA) technology, while PVOIL and the Vietnam Petroleum Institute (VPI) are researching used cooking oil (UCO) alongside alternative feedstocks.

PVOIL Trans has also engaged in collecting UCO and gained operational experience regarding ISCC EU certification. Meanwhile, BSR has successfully blended and sold a fuel consignment containing 5% SAF by combining imported SAF with its own domestically produced Jet A-1.

On the import and distribution side, Vietnam has achieved several milestones. According to the CAAV report, Petrolimex Aviation imported and supplied SAF for Vietjet flights departing from Tan Son Nhat International Airport in 2024 and engaged in SAF blending operations in 2025.

At Noi Bai International Airport, Noi Bai Aviation Fuel Service JSC (NAFSC) conducted an initial assessment indicating that existing infrastructure could potentially handle neat SAF or SAF-blended Jet A-1. However, the company highlighted the need for further evaluations concerning the compatibility of storage tanks, pipelines, equipment, and hydrant systems, as well as standards for quality, testing, certification, and traceability.

The CAAV noted that while Vietnam has established an initial foundation and gained early experience across parts of the SAF value chain, current activities do not yet constitute a fully integrated supply chain. Consequently, insufficient data exists to fully evaluate the feasibility of nationwide SAF deployment.

As the policy framework develops, the CAAV stated it is collaborating with energy firms, fuel distributors, and airlines on drafting committees for the relevant circulars. This ongoing collaboration enables industry stakeholders to provide direct input on the production, export, import, and consumption of SAF, as well as emissions reduction frameworks and carbon offsetting obligations under the Carbon Offsetting and Reduction Scheme for International Aviation (CORSIA).

text:
Metro Atlanta Chamber, Georgia Farm Bureau, Georgia Forestry Association and Delta Air Lines Launch Georgia SAF Coalition

ATLANTA, Sept. 30, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- Georgia agriculture and forestry producers and the business community have teamed up to create the Georgia Sustainable Aviation Fuel (SAF) Coalition, a new partnership focused on positioning the state as a national leader in sustainable aviation fuel research and production. Founding organizations include the Metro Atlanta Chamber, Georgia Farm Bureau, Georgia Forestry Association, and Delta Air Lines, working together to accelerate domestic production of biofuels that utilize Georgia grown agriculture and forestry feedstocks.

Sustainable aviation fuel can be produced from a variety of feedstocks to reduce emissions from air transportation and is designed to be compatible with existing aircraft and fueling infrastructure. While SAF currently represents a small share of global fuel supply, demand is rising quickly across global markets as production scales and interest from airlines and customers continues to accelerate.

Thanks to strong political and business leadership, Georgia has built a foundation to grow the capacity needed to produce ag- and forestry-derived SAF. The Georgia SAF Coalition aims to accelerate that growth by better coordinating public-private partnerships, more closely aligning university research with industry needs, and considering avenues to attract investment.

The coalition's launch builds on the momentum of Georgia's Keep Georgia Forested Act, which encourages investment in forestry manufacturing, including the production of biofuels from Georgia-based feedstocks. The legislation, signed into law by Gov. Brian Kemp in May 2026, enhances Georgia's competitiveness by allowing certain tax credits to be transferred. This change allows companies to monetize credits during the critical early stages of construction and operations, when workers are being hired and capital needs are highest. That investment reaches beyond aviation, creating new markets for Georgia farmers and forest landowners and sustaining demand for locally grown feedstocks.

Georgia's combination of agriculture and forestry resources, world-class research institutions, logistics infrastructure, and industry leadership positions the state to become a leader in sustainable aviation fuel development and production.

"This is about aligning Georgia's natural strengths with real market demand," said Katie Kirkpatrick, President and CEO of the Metro Atlanta Chamber. "Georgia is making a serious play for a piece of the emerging sustainable aviation fuel market. By bringing global companies, producers, researchers, and the agricultural community all to the same table, we are building a powerful biofuels ecosystem that serves the entire state and connects us to the world."

"For farmers across Georgia, sustainable aviation fuel could open new markets for our agricultural commodities, offering new opportunities and increased profitability," said Tom McCall, President of Georgia Farm Bureau. "Partnerships like the Georgia SAF Coalition help connect broader economic innovation to agriculture, the number one industry in our state."

"Georgia is the number one forestry state in the nation, and our state's 22 million acres of working forests are among the most productive in the world," said Tim Lowrimore, President & CEO, Georgia Forestry Association. "SAF provides a chance to put that resource to work in a growing market which means new demand for landowners, new jobs in rural Georgia and new manufacturing investment in the communities that need it most. This coalition makes sure producers are at the table from day one."

"Georgia is well positioned to become a national leader in SAF," said Peter Carter, President of Delta Air Lines. "The Georgia SAF Coalition unites organizations committed to advancing that opportunity. Together, we can power the growth of a SAF industry that strengthens Georgia's economy, supports innovation, and creates lasting benefits for communities across the state."

"Sustainable aviation fuel represents a significant opportunity for the nation's agricultural and forestry sectors and the rural communities that support them. The Georgia SAF Coalition brings together producers, industry leaders and other stakeholders to help unlock new markets, drive innovation and strengthen American energy leadership. Georgia has the resources and expertise to play an important role in the future of SAF while creating economic opportunities across the state. I am glad to see the public-private partnerships behind the effort to allow Sustainable Aviation Fuel to take flight," said Stephen Vaden, Deputy Secretary, U.S. Department of Agriculture.

Prior to launch, coalition members joined the Georgia Research Alliance in successfully advocating for state funding for a Georgia Research Alliance Eminent Scholar. This research will focus on the forestry sector and help identify emerging opportunities, including biofuels.

text:
India has strong foundations to emerge as a major Sustainable Aviation Fuel (SAF) producer, backed by abundant feedstock, established biofuel and refining capabilities and growing investment in SAF technologies, according to a new assessment by the Roundtable on Sustainable Biomaterials (RSB).

The Assessing India’s Readiness for Sustainable Aviation Fuel report gives India an overall SAF readiness score of 52%, placing it in the “moderate” category while highlighting progress towards commercial-scale deployment. The country performs particularly strongly in feedstock availability, SAF production capacity and technology readiness.

India has set indicative SAF blending targets of 1% by 2027, 2% by 2028 and 5% by 2030. Under the 5% blending scenario covering domestic and international aviation, SAF demand could reach about 720 million litres annually by 2030, or around 0.6 million tonnes.

The assessment says India’s theoretical production potential is considerably higher, with studies estimating 14–33 million tonnes of SAF a year based on available feedstock resources. The challenge is therefore less about resource availability and more about developing the systems needed to turn that potential into reliable commercial supply.

Feedstock received the report’s highest readiness score at 78%, while SAF production capacity and technology readiness each scored 60%.

The report identifies HEFA (Hydroprocessed Esters and Fatty Acids) as an important near-term pathway and Alcohol-to-Jet (AtJ) as a key medium- and long-term pathway. Indian companies and oil marketing companies including IOCL, BPCL, MRPL, HPCL, Essar Future Energy and TruAlt Bioenergy are pursuing SAF projects.

Praj Industries, in collaboration with LanzaJet, has commissioned a 1-kilolitre-per-day AtJ demonstration facility in Pune. Praj and IOCL also operated a commercial Pune-Delhi flight in 2023 using an indigenously produced SAF blend.

The weaker areas identified by the assessment include market demand (30%), investment and financing (40%), enabling infrastructure and services (40%) and supply chain and logistics (45%). Policy and regulation scored 53%.

Agricultural residues are often dispersed among farmers, while waste oils and municipal waste face collection and segregation challenges. The report calls for stronger aggregation, transport and storage systems, including regional logistics hubs and digital traceability.

The RSB also recommends moving from indicative to binding SAF blending mandates, including domestic aviation, developing a national SAF roadmap and introducing SAF-specific financial mechanisms such as viability-gap funding, tax incentives and contracts for difference.

The report proposes a three-stage pathway: first, moving towards 1–2% blending and commercial SAF plants; second, scaling towards 5% blending by 2030; and finally developing India into a globally integrated, export-oriented SAF producer with internationally aligned certification and traceability systems.

The assessment concludes that India’s 52% score reflects momentum constrained by structural gaps rather than a lack of technical or resource potential. Closing those gaps will require coordinated action by government, industry, investors, researchers and international partners.

The Cardano Foundation announced two research projects on Wednesday—one focused on sustainable aviation fuel (SAF), a low-carbon alternative that can be used in existing aircraft and airports, and another targeting Diesel R, a diesel fuel partially produced by Petrobras using renewable feedstocks such as vegetable oils and animal fats. The aviation fuel project addresses the book-and-claim model used in green fuel sales: airlines can pay for the environmental benefits of sustainable fuel even when the physical fuel is consumed elsewhere. This model requires precise tracking of who claims the benefits and when, to prevent double-counting of emissions reductions. The application uses Cardano to record the origin, recipient, and claim time of each benefit. In practical use, passengers could input their departure and destination airports to calculate corresponding fuel benefits and receive a verifiable credential linking their allocation to the original fuel certificate. The diesel project records data across all stages of fuel production, transportation, and usage, compiling a comprehensive lifecycle traceability record that supports corporate reporting of Scope 3 emissions. Frederik Gregaard, CEO of the Cardano Foundation, noted that Brazil has been one of Cardano’s most consistent adopters—from government agencies like SERPRO to industrial institutions like SENAI—and that Petrobras continues to value on-chain traceability and transparency. He added that institutional interest is growing as x402 launches on Cardano and Fireblocks adds support for native Cardano tokens.

title: How Europe can build stronger military fuel resilience - Topsoe
description:
Refinery capacity is decreasing, fossil fuel supply chains are increasingly exposed to geopolitical risk, and long-term fuel availability can no longer be taken for granted.
The Hague Centre for Strategic Studies (HCSS) has published a white paper on how alternative fuels can support European military fuel readiness.

text:
As Europe moves through the energy transition, the fuel system that has supported military operations for decades is changing. Refinery capacity is decreasing, fossil fuel supply chains are increasingly exposed to geopolitical risk, and long-term fuel availability can no longer be taken for granted.

The Hague Centre for Strategic Studies (HCSS) has published a white paper on how alternative fuels can support European military fuel readiness. Topsoe contributed technical input and recommendations to the paper.

The central message is clear: alternative fuels can strengthen European military resilience – especially Sustainable Aviation Fuel (SAF) and e-SAF made from renewable power – and the transition should be phased-in now to preserve European military readiness, inter-operability and operational flexibility in the long term.

Fuel readiness is becoming a strategic issue

Europe’s armed forces have historically relied on conventional fuels supplied through established refinery and logistics systems. But that model is under pressure.

The conflict in the Middle East this year created the largest oil supply disruption in history and exposed Europe’s fuel vulnerability. The closure of the Strait of Hormuz and attacks on regional oil infrastructure have had major consequences for global oil prices and supply security and have cost Europe nearly EUR 500 million per day – on top of the roughly EUR 340 billion Europe already spends annually on fuel imports.

Around 60% of the European Union’s energy is imported, and around half of imported jet fuel comes from the Middle East. That fuel is not only essential to commercial aviation. It is also the principal NATO military fuel.

According to the white paper, a broader and faster adoption of alternative fuels can improve supply chain diversification and strengthen Europe’s strategic autonomy, though there are short-term trade-offs related to cost, standardization and interoperability.

The white paper also points to an important practical advantage: synthetic drop-in fuels can be used directly in aircrafts such as F-16 and F-35 without any engine modifications or changes in the current fuel systems.

Why drop-in synthetic fuels matter

For defense applications, compatibility is essential. Fuels must meet strict performance requirements, such as NATO's fuel specifications and work reliably under existing operating conditions.

Here, synthetic drop-in fuels offer a practical pathway. They can be used in existing engines and infrastructure without modifications, aside from the mandatory military additives - corrosion inhibitor, static dissipator and fuel icing inhibitor - that is also added to kerosene - and blended with fossil fuels, creating flexibility at a time of geopolitical uncertainty and supply chain strain.

This creates a realistic route to stronger military fuel resilience. Domestic and regional production of synthetic fuels such as e-SAF can shorten supply chains, reduce dependence on imported fossil fuels, and support greater European fuel autonomy. For military users, that can mean stronger security of supply in both peacetime and crises.

Policy can help scale supply

The technologies needed to produce synthetic drop-in fuels already exist. The challenge is scaling production fast enough to meet both civilian and strategic demand.

If Europe wants a more resilient fuel system, policy must help create the conditions for investment. That means supporting industrial development, enabling long-term offtake and recognizing alternative fuels as part of Europe’s security infrastructure.

This is not only relevant to defense. Building industrial-scale production capacity for synthetic fuels can create a more flexible energy system that supports civilian transport, strategic industries, and military needs alike. In that sense, fuel resilience and industrial policy are closely linked.

Three recommendations for policymakers

To strengthen European military fuel readiness while keeping pace with civilian market developments, the paper makes three recommendations for policymakers in European NATO member states:

Create a joint civil-military strategy for alternative fuels

Fuel infrastructure in Europe is largely civilian-owned, while military demand is limited in peacetime but could become critical in a crisis. Better coordination is needed on information sharing, demand planning, infrastructure and investment gaps, led by national governments and supported by the EU and NATO.

Treat alternative fuel plants as dual-use strategic assets

Governments should support the scale-up of alternative fuels by reducing investment risk and creating stronger demand signals. This could include reservation agreements, long-term offtake contracts or public ownership stakes in fuel plants, with funding potentially coming from NATO defense infrastructure spending or EU climate-related budgets.

Set benchmarks for minimum domestic production capacity

The 2026 Middle East oil disruption showed that fuel security depends not just on supply, but also on access, control and location. Europe should secure a minimum level of domestic production capacity for alternative fuels, feedstocks and related technologies to avoid overdependence on foreign suppliers.

From analysis to action

Alternative fuels are not a silver bullet, and the paper is clear that short-term trade-offs must be managed carefully. But it also shows that phased, targeted adoption can improve resilience, diversify supply and strengthen strategic autonomy over time.

For European decision-makers, the implication is straightforward: military fuel readiness must become part of the broader conversation on defense, energy security and industrial competitiveness.

Europe cannot afford to treat fuel as a background issue. It is a strategic capability. Strengthening it will require coordinated action from policymakers, industry, and defense actors alike.

text:
Biofuels are necessary in helping to decarbonize the entire transport sector, from which around 20% of global emissions are generated. From bioethanol for cars to SAF for planes, the entire fuel market is being re-evaluated in a light of sustainability. IDTechEx's portfolio of Sustainability Research Reports and Subscriptions covers an entire range of initiatives which aim to significantly lower harmful emissions.

Bioethanol, biodiesel, and advanced biofuels

Although electric vehicles are one solution to decarbonizing road transport covered in IDTechEx's portfolio of Electric Vehicles Research Reports and Subscriptions, for the wider transportation landscape including aviation and shipping, electrification is not a feasible option. Low-carbon fuels, many of which can be drop-in fuels requiring minimal infrastructure changes, will therefore be a better-suited alternative. Bioethanol and biodiesel are also already used globally for cars in gasoline and diesel blends, to reduce the number of harmful emissions created from existing combustion engine vehicles. IDTechEx's report, "Sustainable Biofuels & E-Fuels Market 2026-2036: Technologies, Players, Forecasts", goes into further detail.

Bioethanol is mostly created from sugarcane, while biodiesel is traditionally made from vegetable oils, meaning both are created from natural feedstocks rather than coming from fossil fuels. However, one of the main issues with these feedstocks is the high land and water usage required in their production, which can come at the cost of deforestation and loss of biodiversity. Many traditional 1st generation biofuels are therefore also still responsible for a significant amount of greenhouse gas emissions. According to IDTechEx, government subsidies are now shifting more towards the production of advanced biofuels and e-fuels that generate even less emissions, and as a result, scalability of 1st generation biofuels is currently limited.

Advanced biofuels encompass 2nd, 3rd, and 4th generation biofuels. 2nd generation biofuels are created from lignocellulose or waste biomass and vegetable oils, as to recycle pre-used materials and to not demand excess land usage, while 3rd generation biofuels are expected to be made from algae, and 4th generation from genetically engineered microorganisms, algae, or even captured CO2. IDTechEx's report, "Industrial Biomanufacturing 2027-2037: Technologies, Markets, Players, Forecasts", report covers a whole range of biomanufacturing routes and applications including fuels.

SAF, HEFA, and alcohol-to-jet fuel

Sustainable aviation fuel (SAF) for planes is one market seeing significant growth and investment. SAF is created via the HEFA (hydrotreated esters and fatty acids) route, which sees oils and other waste materials treated with hydrogen to remove oxygen and collect hydrocarbons which are chemically the same as regular diesel or kerosene. Globally, there is reportedly a few million tonnes of HEFA- SAF capacity a year, with IDTechEx forecasting the global SAF market to reach US$50 billion in 2036.

Alcohol-to-jet is an alternative biofuel pathway, which sees ethanol or methanol being upgraded to hydrocarbon fuels, which can then be blended with regular jet fuel. This process sees ethanol and methanol undergoing dehydration, oligomerization, hydrogenation and isomerization, and finally fractional distillation. Details of these processes can be found in IDTechEx's "Sustainable Biofuels & E-Fuels Market" report.

Many companies have already begun commercial operation of alcohol-to-jet fuel which IDTechEx states will pave the way for even bigger SAF production capabilities. One of LanzaJet's facilities has been reported to produce 9 million gallons of SAF and 1 million gallons of renewable diesel a year, highlighting the great scope for further growth within the market and encouraging many other companies to follow suit.

text:
Hanoi (VNS/VNA) - Vietnam is studying domestic feedstocks and technologies for producing sustainable aviation fuel (SAF) as the country is accelerating the development of a roadmap to gradually introduce the fuel into the country's aviation market, the Civil Aviation Authority of Vietnam (CAAV) said.

The authority is surveying available feedstocks including agricultural biomass, used cooking oil and waste, as well as suitable conversion technologies.

In a recent report to the Ministry of Construction, the CAAV said its findings will be used to propose a SAF supply chain model, management measures and a phased roadmap for deployment in Vietnam.

The proposed SAF roadmap will take into account Vietnam's international commitments, the Carbon Offsetting and Reduction Scheme for International Aviation (CORSIA) and the country's ability to develop a domestic SAF supply, while avoiding shocks to domestic airlines and the air transport market.

Vietnam has already gained initial experience in importing, supplying and using SAF, while some energy companies are also examining opportunities to produce SAF domestically.

Petrolimex Aviation imported and supplied SAF for Vietjet flights at Tan Son Nhat International Airport in 2024 and participated in SAF blending in 2025.

Vietnam Airlines used 2,200 tonnes of SAF in 2025, reducing lifecycle carbon emissions by about 5,600 tonnes, the carrier said. In May 2024, it operated a commercial passenger flight from Singapore to Hanoi using SAF, becoming the first Vietnamese airline to use the fuel on a commercial passenger flight.

On August 15, Vietjet used SAF produced by Petrolimex Aviation on its flights. Petrolimex Aviation blended and supplied 1,200cu.m of SAF for Vietjet flights.

PetroVietnam has assigned its subsidiaries, Bình Sơn Refining and Petrochemical JSC (BSR) and PetroVietnam Oil Corporation (PVOIL), to work on SAF production.

BSR has studied producing SAF using the hydroprocessed esters and fatty acids technology, while PVOIL and the Vietnam Petroleum Institute have studied used cooking oil and other potential feedstocks.

To sustain long-term growth, airlines belonging to the International Air Transport Association have set a goal of achieving net zero emissions by 2050, with SAF expected to account for up to 65 per cent of the emissions reductions needed to meet that target.

However, the CAAV said airlines' readiness remained uneven, with some carriers lacking specific SAF plans or sufficient information to assess their ability to deploy the fuel. In addition, existing activities had yet to form a complete SAF supply chain, and there was not enough information to fully assess the feasibility of deploying SAF nationwide.

Airport fuel infrastructure is an important part of the SAF supply chain, according to the CAAV.

At Noi Bài International Airport in Hanoi, the local aviation fuel service company has initially assessed that existing infrastructure could potentially be used for SAF or Jet A-1 blended with SAF.

Still, further assessments are needed to determine the compatibility of storage tanks, pipelines, equipment and refuelling systems, while requirements for fuel quality, testing, certification and traceability also need to be clarified.

The CAAV said it would continue working with Petrovietnam and Petrolimex on SAF production and deployment in Vietnam.

At a September 2025 meeting of the provisional Joint Committee for the ASEAN-EU Comprehensive Air Transport Agreement in Bangkok, ASEAN countries asked the EU to consider allowing SAF to be certified under both the EU's RefuelEU Aviation framework and ICAO's CORSIA standards.

Vietnam would continue to participate in discussions aimed at harmonising SAF recognition between EU and ICAO mechanisms in order to facilitate implementation by domestic carriers, the CAAV said.

CAAV Director Uong Viet Dung said that the launch of SAF would be strategically important for the long term, because it would lay the groundwork for a sustainable domestic SAF supply chain which meets international market requirements and encourages cooperation among airlines, fuel suppliers, regulators and financial institutions.

SAF is produced from renewable and sustainably sourced materials such as used cooking oil, agricultural residues, woody biomass and municipal waste. It can reduce lifecycle carbon emissions compared with conventional jet fuel./.

title: ARC Bio Demonstrates Canadian Forest Residue Pathway to Sustainable Aviation Fuel
description:
The project upgraded fast pyrolysis bio-oil produced from Canadian forest residues by Bioénergie AECN in Port-Cartier into barrel-scale quantities of Alder Renewable Crude (ARC).
"We demonstrated a pathway connecting Canadian forest residues with refinery infrastructure already operating at commercial scale.
The project also demonstrates opportunities to create value from low-value woody biomass, including forest residues generated through forest management and wildfire-risk reduction, where appropriate feedstock supply chains can be established.
Leveraging Refinery Infrastructure Already in Place Unlike pathways requiring an entirely new standalone fuel refinery, ARC Bio's approach is designed to integrate with existing refinery operations.
About ARC Bio and its Partners ARC Bio is a Canadian joint venture between an affiliated company of Bioénergie AECN and Alder Renewables focused on converting Canadian forest residues into renewable fuels.
text:
Pilot-scale refinery co-processing demonstrates a pathway to convert forest industry residues into low-carbon jet fuel using existing infrastructure.

PORT-CARTIER, QC, Sept. 30, 2026 /CNW/ -- ARC Bio, the Canadian joint venture between an affiliate of Bioénergie AE Cote-Nord Canada Inc. ("Bioénergie AECN") and Alder Renewables, today announced the successful demonstration of a pathway to produce sustainable aviation fuel ("SAF") from Canadian forest residues through refinery co-processing.

The demonstration brings together Canada's forest products industry, renewable fuels technology and existing refining infrastructure to show how residual woody biomass can be converted into a refinery-ready biocrude for processing alongside conventional feedstocks to produce transportation fuels, including SAF.

"Canada has the biomass feedstock, the forest sector expertise, the industrial capability and the refining infrastructure to build an important new clean fuel value chain," said Serge Mercier, President of Bioénergie AECN. "This work creates a direct connection between Canada's forest sector economy and the growing need for low-carbon fuels in aviation and marine transportation markets."

The project upgraded fast pyrolysis bio-oil produced from Canadian forest residues by Bioénergie AECN in Port-Cartier into barrel-scale quantities of Alder Renewable Crude (ARC). This biocrude was then processed in a fluid catalytic cracking, or FCC, pilot unit that simulates commercial refinery operation. Carbon-14 analysis of the resulting fuel products confirmed the presence of biogenic carbon from the wood residue-derived feedstock.

The FCC campaign successfully produced a jet-range fuel fraction that was isolated and evaluated for blending compatibility with HEFA-based SAF produced from fats, oils and greases. The resulting SAF blend met the key ASTM D1655 fuel-property specifications evaluated in the screening. The work represents an important step toward demonstrating that biocrude produced from Canadian forest residues can enter existing refinery infrastructure and be converted into finished transportation fuels.

"The significance of this demonstration is not simply that we produced a renewable jet-range fuel," said Derek Vardon, CEO of Alder Renewables. "We demonstrated a pathway connecting Canadian forest residues with refinery infrastructure already operating at commercial scale. That creates the potential for a scalable, capital-efficient route to bring forest-derived renewable carbon into aviation fuel markets."

With financial support from Boeing, the project was established to validate the conversion of forest residues into SAF in Canada and generate the technical and economic data needed to support future commercial-scale facilities.

A New Market Opportunity for Canada's Forest Sector

Canada's forest industry generates large volumes of wood residues. As traditional markets face changing demand and international trade pressures, creating higher-value uses for these residues can strengthen forest-sector economics while supplying renewable carbon to industries that are difficult to decarbonize.

The project also demonstrates opportunities to create value from low-value woody biomass, including forest residues generated through forest management and wildfire-risk reduction, where appropriate feedstock supply chains can be established.

By converting these materials into an energy-dense, transportable biocrude, ARC Bio is developing a model that connects distributed forestry resources with large-scale fuel refining infrastructure.

Leveraging Refinery Infrastructure Already in Place

Unlike pathways requiring an entirely new standalone fuel refinery, ARC Bio's approach is designed to integrate with existing refinery operations. Fluid catalytic cracking is widely used in refineries around the world to produce transportation fuel components. Introducing Alder Renewable Crude into an FCC process creates a pathway connecting renewable feedstocks with existing commercial fuel production assets.

The next stage of the program will generate additional refinery-relevant data to support larger-scale trials. ARC Bio's roadmap is ultimately aimed at enabling a first-of-a-kind Canadian commercial project combining forest-residue conversion, biocrude production and refinery integration.

Learn more about ARC Bio's milestone and latest activities at ARC Bio News.

About ARC Bio and its Partners

ARC Bio is a Canadian joint venture between an affiliated company of Bioénergie AECN and Alder Renewables focused on converting Canadian forest residues into renewable fuels. The collaboration combines commercial fast pyrolysis, renewable crude upgrading, and refinery processing to advance sustainable aviation fuel and marine fuels in Canada. Bioénergie AECN operates North America's largest fast pyrolysis bio-oil facility using wood residue feedstocks in Port-Cartier, Quebec. The Port-Cartier facility has an annual production capacity of 40 million litres of bio-oil. Alder Renewables develops upgrading technology that converts fast pyrolysis bio-oil into refinery-ready biocrude for downstream production of low-carbon fuels and other industrial products.

title: India records 52% SAF readiness as Boeing-RSB report outlines adoption roadmap
description:
India has recorded an overall Sustainable Aviation Fuel (SAF) readiness score of 52 per cent , indicating moderate but advancing preparedness for wider SAF adoption, according to a new report by Boeing and the Roundtable on Sustainable Biomaterials (RSB).
India has set SAF blending targets of 1 per cent by 2027, 2 per cent by 2028 and 5 per cent by 2030.
The assessment also highlights that production potential alone will not determine the pace of SAF adoption.
“This report is valuable because it confirms exactly where India has the foundational capacity to enable SAF adoption and because it identifies specific opportunities ahead,” Gupte added.
The assessment comes as India’s aviation sector continues to expand, increasing the relevance of scalable lower-carbon fuel options for meeting the sector’s longer-term emissions reduction objectives.
text: India has recorded an overall Sustainable Aviation Fuel (SAF) readiness score of 52 per cent , indicating moderate but advancing preparedness for wider SAF adoption, according to a new report by Boeing and the Roundtable on Sustainable Biomaterials (RSB). The report assesses India’s readiness across nine dimensions, including feedstock availability, production capacity, policy and regulation, supply chains and logistics, market demand, investment and financing, research and development, technology readiness, and enabling infrastructure and services. India has set SAF blending targets of 1 per cent by 2027, 2 per cent by 2028 and 5 per cent by 2030. The country is also committed to participating in the International Civil Aviation Organization’s Carbon Offsetting and Reduction Scheme for International Aviation (CORSIA) from 2027. Under a 5 per cent SAF blending scenario in 2030, demand across domestic and international aviation is projected at around 720 million litres, or approximately 0.6 million tonnes, annually. The report estimates India’s potential SAF production capacity at 14-33 million tonnes per year, indicating significant potential supply capacity relative to projected demand under the scenario. The assessment also highlights that production potential alone will not determine the pace of SAF adoption. Development of supporting infrastructure, supply chains, financing, policy frameworks and market demand will be important to establishing a wider SAF ecosystem. “As one of the world’s fastest-growing aviation markets, India has an important role in enabling sustainable aviation - and pursuing a deliberate and well-researched path to SAF adoption is key,” said Salil Gupte, president, Boeing India & South Asia. “This report is valuable because it confirms exactly where India has the foundational capacity to enable SAF adoption and because it identifies specific opportunities ahead,” Gupte added. RSB said the assessment is intended to provide stakeholders with a common evidence base for developing India’s SAF market and identifying areas requiring further coordination. “India's Sustainable Aviation Fuel opportunity is substantial. This assessment gives stakeholders a common evidence base from which to act, and RSB looks forward to continuing to convene and support the collaboration needed to translate India's potential into sustainable impact,” said Bettina Paschke, Executive Director, RSB. The report points to coordinated action among government, aviation companies, financiers and other stakeholders as a key requirement for developing the SAF market. Boeing said it will continue to support airline customers and policymakers in India and globally in efforts to develop a SAF ecosystem and address aviation emissions. The assessment comes as India’s aviation sector continues to expand, increasing the relevance of scalable lower-carbon fuel options for meeting the sector’s longer-term emissions reduction objectives.

text:
Today the first A350F aircraft – MSN700 – took to the skies for the very first time. This flight marked the beginning of the planned 10 month / 400 flight hour test campaign which will culminate in EASA Type Certification – paving the way to first customer deliveries of the world’s most efficient widebody freighter. As a new member of the A350 Family, A350F will deliver up to 40% lower fuel burn and CO₂ emissions compared with previous-generation freighters.

The crew of five on board were: Experimental Test Pilots Bernardo Saez-Benito Hernandez and Sylvain Guiraud; Test-Flight Engineer (TFE) Ludovic Girard; and Flight-Test-Engineers (FTEs) Laurent Bussiere and Jaime Angoloti Benavides.

Over the coming months, many more of Airbus’ flight test professionals will take part in the global certification flight test campaign – which feature two the complementary test aircraft:

MSN700 will focus on handling qualities, autopilot systems and performance. This aircraft has been equipped with a specialised tail skid and bumper to protect the structure (from a potential contact with the runway) during the take-off performance tests.

MSN701, meanwhile, will focus on system-related testing, including air conditioning, water & waste and comprehensive smoke detection testing. MSN701 will also perform the hot and cold weather campaign as well as visiting customers.

As of today, MSN701 has completed final assembly and is undergoing ground tests before entering the paintshop.

Celebrating a collective engineering excellence

Julien Puyou, Airbus’ Head of Widebody Programme comments: “From a bold vision on paper in 2021 to seeing the A350F fly for the first time today, this milestone is a triumph of pioneering spirit and collective determination.”

He adds: “Looking back at where we started when we launched the A350F programme, turning a revolutionary composite freighter design into physical reality has been an extraordinary human and industrial journey. Seeing our teams across Europe and beyond deliver breakthrough engineering – from delivering the largest main-deck cargo door in commercial aviation, conducting detailed large demonstrator testing, FAL final assembly, flight test instrumentation installation, ground testing, virtual development simulations and now the first flight in Toulouse – demonstrates what we can achieve when we unite around a shared goal."

What took place in the first flight?

The crew flew the aircraft for 4 hours and 10 minutes, during which they explored the aircraft’s handling characteristics in direct law, the engines’ behaviour, and core mechanical systems. The aircraft reached an indicated airspeed (IAS) of 340 kts and an altitude of 25,000 ft.

Validating control laws against predictive models

The main objective of the initial flight is to validate and clear the aircraft's control laws by comparing real-time flight performance against the pre-flight predictive models that established the handling qualities. To this end, the crew took off in direct law which provides direct manual control.

They progressively climbed to 10,000ft then to 25,000 ft to evaluate the aircraft’s behaviour and confirmed that the aircraft’s actual aerodynamics and structural model matched the models which the crew had previously flown in the simulator. Once this had been achieved, and everything was within acceptable thresholds, normal law was activated, in order to clear the flying aircraft with its full flight envelope protections, and across the normal speed range.

Validating primary systems in flight

Aside from confirming the aerodynamic and structural characteristics, the crew also evaluated the primary systems such as pressurisation (measuring potential leakage rates against ground baseline tests), communication, and navigation to ensure they functioned as expected, thus paving the way to launching the broader flight test campaign in subsequent flights.

Real-time telemetry and the Flight Test Instrumentation (FTI) suite

Key to the aircraft's role as a flight-test vehicle is its Flight Test Instrumentation (FTI) suite – developed by Airbus’ own Electrical Centre in Toulouse and integrated into the fuselage sections in Airbus Atlantic in Montoir-de-Bretagne and Airbus Aerostructures in Hamburg. During a flight test the FTI tracks thousands of parameters on-board and conveys telemetry to monitoring teams on the ground in real time.

After the flight, Laurent Bussiere, lead flight test engineer enthused: “We are now starting the flight test campaign and we're all very proud to be part of today’s mission. For all of us it’s a real milestone to be part of the first flight crew of a new aircraft. This aircraft is exceptional – its payload capabilities, fuel efficiency and flexibility show that it really will be a top freighter aircraft for all the airlines who will operate it.”

text:
PTI

Updated On Sep 30, 2026 at 09:30 AM IST

Jet fuel demand in India would rise from about 192,000 barrels per day in 2024 to 277,000 barrels per day by 2031, providing a strong market for the Sustainable Aviation Fuel (SAF), as per a report released on Monday.

The government has announced SAF blending roadmap starting with 1 per cent blending in 2027 and increasing to 2 per cent in 2028 and 5 per cent in 2030 to decarbonise the aviation industry.

Advt

The report jointly developed by S&P Global Energy and the SAF Association estimates that the SAF demand will be 46,000 tonne in 2027, which would rise to 250,000 tonne in 2030.

India's aviation sector is expected to remain one of the fastest-growing sources of refined product demand through 2060, providing a strong foundation for developing a domestic SAF market, the report said.

"This expansion is driven by rising middle-class mobility, continued growth in domestic and international air travel, airport infrastructure development, and ongoing airline fleet additions," it said.

The report, released at 2nd India SAF Conclave, noted that while some short-term weakness emerged in 2026, particularly in the international segment, the underlying demand trajectory remains firmly positive.

Advt

India's aviation fuel consumption softened in mid-2026, with July demand falling to about 180,000 barrel per day reflecting weaker flight activity, higher operating costs, and supply-side disruptions, it said.

However, first-half 2026 jet fuel consumption still increased by nearly 2 per cent year-over-year, suggesting the recent slowdown is temporary rather than structural and does not alter the longer-term growth outlook, the report said.

"The demand outlook is further supported by rising passenger traffic, the continued expansion of low-cost aviation, and increasing international connectivity," it said.

New infrastructure, including Navi Mumbai International Airport and Jewar Airport in Noida, is expected to ease capacity constraints and support additional growth in flight activity.

International aviation is likely to remain an important demand driver, with international seat capacity expanding faster than domestic capacity in 2026 despite higher ticket costs.

"Policy support is also expected to play an important role in sustaining aviation growth. A key structural driver is the government's continued focus on expanding air connectivity through UDAN (Ude Desh Ka Aam Nagrik) Regional Connectivity Scheme," the report said.

It highlighted that the government has introduced an aviation turbine fuel (ATF) pricing stabilization mechanism, including a fixed ATF price in Delhi and a dedicated stabilization fund.

While not a direct subsidy, the mechanism reduces fuel price volatility and improves cost visibility for airlines, it added.

text:
Plug Power Inc. PLUG stock gained Tuesday after the hydrogen technology company signed a strategic partnership with Arcadia eFuels covering more than 1 gigawatt of potential electrolyzer projects.

The agreement includes a 280-megawatt electrolyzer supply deal for Arcadia’s Project ENDOR in Denmark. It also positions Plug as the preferred electrolyzer supplier for four additional projects in Europe and the Americas.

Plug Power Lands 280-MW Denmark Project

Project ENDOR is planned for the Port of Vordingborg on Denmark’s south coast. The facility will use renewable electricity to power 280 MW of Plug’s GenEco electrolyzers.

Plug said the equipment is expected to produce about 110 tons of renewable hydrogen per day. Arcadia plans to combine the hydrogen with captured carbon dioxide to produce synthetic sustainable aviation fuel, or e-SAF, for conventional aircraft.

Deliveries will begin after the project issues a notice to proceed. Arcadia said ENDOR is advancing toward a final investment decision. The agreement follows three years of engineering work between the companies.

See More: Top Value Stocks

Partnership Expands Beyond ENDOR

The broader cooperation agreement gives Arcadia priority access to Plug’s manufacturing capacity as future projects advance. The planned pipeline represents more than 1 GW of potential electrolyzer capacity.

Plug CEO José Luis Crespo said Europe remains the company’s most active electrolyzer market. He also pointed to growing e-SAF demand as European aviation fuel mandates take effect.

The European Union’s ReFuelEU Aviation rules require airlines and fuel suppliers to increase the use of sustainable aviation fuels. The regulation also introduces a synthetic aviation fuel requirement beginning in 2030.

Plug is already working on several large European hydrogen projects, including a 100-MW GenEco installation at Galp’s Sines refinery in Portugal.

Analyst Reiterates Buy Rating

Separately, HC Wainwright analyst Amit Dayal on Tuesday reiterated a Buy rating on Plug Power and maintained a $7 price target.

text:
Climate technology firm Aether Fuels has successfully constructed, commissioned, and operated its integrated sustainable aviation fuel (SAF) technology platform at its Chicago, Illinois research and development (R&D) facility.

The demonstration line combines the company’s 2.5 barrel-per-day (bpd) Aurora tri-converter and upgrader units, integrated together with North Carolina technology development firm RTI’s existing Fischer-Tropsch reactor in a key step towards scale-up and commercial validation.

It used Kentucky landfill-derived renewable natural gas (RNG) and industrial captured carbon dioxide (CO2) feedstocks in an electrified syngas generation process to produce SAF meeting ASTM D7566 specification. The production was certified by third-party AmSpec.

Aether Fuels believes it is the first company in North America to produce SAF from mass-balanced RNG and captured industrial CO2 at scale, in line with ASTM standards.

Under the ASTM D7566 specification, alternative fuels can be blended with conventional kerosene up to 50% without requiring modification to existing aircraft tanks, pipelines, or airport fueling systems.

Conor Madigan, CEO and co-founder of Aether Fuels, said the company started with a pilot demonstration, then scaled up over 50 times in standalone demo units, before bringing together the demo units in an integrated line to produce ASTM-standard SAF.

Dhaval Shah, Chief Technology Officer at Aether Fuels, added, “The data from this demonstration informs and de-risks the design of our 50-bpd Project Beacon plant in Singapore, as we continue our rapid journey to large-scale commercial deployment.”

In May, Aether Fuels announced it was partnering with Singapore-based FlyORO Technologies to explore the development of a SAF supply chain, centred on Project Beacon.

Project Beacon is Aether’s planned commercial demonstration facility at the Aster Pulau Bukom refinery in Singapore, which aims to be the first commercial-scale SAF facility in Southeast Asia and will use a more feedstock-flexible route to production using waste carbon.

text:
Christoph Struempfel-Seifert, M.Sc.

Head of airsight’s Sustainable Aviation department

Mr Struempfel-Seifert is an expert for sustainable aviation and is responsible for all project tasks related to sustainable aviation and environmental protection at airports. Furthermore, he is an appreciated trainer, sharing his knowledge and practical experience with other national and international aviation experts.

After graduating as Master of Science in Aeronautics and Astronautics from the Technical University of Berlin, he worked as a research assistant and lecturer at the Chair of Flight Guidance and Air Transport at the TU Berlin. In his scientific career, he focused on modelling aircraft noise and emissions, UAS noise measurements and calculation as well as the optimization of flight procedures with respect to environmental and eco-efficiency targets.

For airsight, he has conducted several environmental assessments, noise and emissions studies for various airports in Germany, Luxembourg, United Arab Emirates, Romania and the Philippines. As a recognized SME for aircraft noise modeling, he has extensive experience with the FAA's Aviation Environmental Design Tool (AEDT).

A second major focus of his work is to support international airports on their decarbonization journey with detailed studies on renewable energy, in particular the implementation of solar energy systems, including Singapore-Changi, Berlin, Cologne, Düsseldorf, Stuttgart and various other airports. His team is helping airports meet the challenges of the future through new, sustainable technologies, such as sustainable aircraft taxiing and e-GSE implementation.

Robert Marx, M.Sc., MBA

Robert Marx is an aerospace engineer and sustainability advocate dedicated to shaping the future of aviation.

With a background in aeronautics and astronautics from the Technische Universität Berlin and an MBA from the University of St. Gallen and Imperial College London, where he focused on sustainable business strategy, he combines deep technical expertise with a strategic approach to implementation.

Robert has gained valuable experience working with industry leaders such as Lufthansa Cargo in Singapore and Boeing’s Future Aircraft Manufacturing Business Unit in Seattle and Puebla. These experiences not only broadened his perspective on the aviation sector but also reinforced the urgency of making air travel more sustainable.

In 2021, he founded the Sustainable Aviation Initiative e.V. (SAI) in Berlin, a non-profit organization dedicated to educating young professionals and fostering collaboration to accelerate aviation’s sustainable transition. SAI has developed an accredited university module on sustainability in aerospace at the University of Stuttgart, covering alternative propulsion systems, sustainable aviation fuels, and regulatory frameworks. The organization also produces the What’s Up Aviation podcast and hosts webinars, bringing together experts to discuss the latest advancements in the field.

Beyond SAI, Robert is passionate about mentoring startups and helping bridge the gap between innovative ideas and real-world application. His work is driven by a clear goal: to push the aviation industry toward more sustainable solutions without compromising its efficiency and connectivity.

title: SkyNRG selects Technip Energies, Sasol, and Topsoe for Project Wigeon FEED
description:
Project Wigeon will combine Topsoe’s SynCOR and hydroprocessing technologies with Sasol’s Fischer-Tropsch technology to convert RNG into SAF.
Technip Energies brings extensive experience working with both Topsoe’s and Sasol’s technologies, alongside strong modularisation capabilities to support the project’s execution.
The appointment also builds on SkyNRG’s established relationship with Technip Energies through DSL-01, SkyNRG’s SAF production facility currently under construction in Delfzijl, the Netherlands.
Steve Drennan, co-president and project director, said“Bringing Technip Energies, Sasol and Topsoe on board is an important step in progressing Project Wigeon toward FEED.
Together, SkyNRG, Technip Energies, Topsoe, Sasol and other project partners, including Boeing, are working to advance Project Wigeon toward commercial-scale SAF production and support the continued growth of advanced SAF supply in North America.
text:
SkyNRG on Sept. 28 announced the selection of Technip Energies, Sasol and Topsoe as key partners for the initial engineering activities of the front-end engineering design (FEED) phase of Project Wigeon, its planned sustainable aviation fuel (SAF) facility at the Port of Walla Walla in Washington State.

The appointments bring together technology and engineering expertise to support Project Wigeon as it progresses into FEED, a key phase in further developing the project’s engineering, cost and execution plans towards a future final investment decision (FID). Project Wigeon is designed to produce 50 million gallons (143 kt) of SAF annually using renewable natural gas (RNG) and commercially proven Fischer-Tropsch technology. With key permitting secured and start-up targeted for 2031, the project aims to add significant new SAF production capacity in North America.

Topsoe and Sasol have each signed a Basic Engineering Design Package agreement with SkyNRG, providing technology licenses, engineering design and technical services for their respective technologies. Project Wigeon will combine Topsoe’s SynCOR and hydroprocessing technologies with Sasol’s Fischer-Tropsch technology to convert RNG into SAF.

Technip Energies brings extensive experience working with both Topsoe’s and Sasol’s technologies, alongside strong modularisation capabilities to support the project’s execution. The appointment also builds on SkyNRG’s established relationship with Technip Energies through DSL-01, SkyNRG’s SAF production facility currently under construction in Delfzijl, the Netherlands.

Steve Drennan, co-president and project director, said“Bringing Technip Energies, Sasol and Topsoe on board is an important step in progressing Project Wigeon toward FEED. Together, we are combining proven technologies with deep engineering and project execution expertise to further develop a permitted, design-ready project and lay the foundations for commercial-scale advanced SAF production in the .US.”

Loïc Chapuis, president project delivery and services at Technip Energies, commented, “Project Wigeon marks a new step in our collaboration with SkyNRG, building on the work already underway on DSL-01 project in the Netherlands. This new milestone demonstrates how our engineering and project delivery expertise can support SkyNRG as it develops SAF projects across different geographies and contributes to the growth of sustainable aviation fuel production.”

The project will be led by Andy Billig, co-president, commercial and external affairs, and Steve Drennan, co-president and project director. Andy will focus on strategic partnerships and stakeholder engagement, while Steve will oversee development and technical delivery. They will work closely with SkyNRG’s wider leadership team, including Jessie van der Linden, VP of projects, who will serve as a key SkyNRG counterpart supporting governance and delivery.

Together, SkyNRG, Technip Energies, Topsoe, Sasol and other project partners, including Boeing, are working to advance Project Wigeon toward commercial-scale SAF production and support the continued growth of advanced SAF supply in North America.

text:
You can make your climate contribution for every Condor or Marabu flight. This contribution will be used proportionately to support the three climate projects by our renowned partner myclimate as well as for increasing our future use of Sustainable Aviation Fuel (SAF) on Condor flights.

Eight different climate packages are available to you. Either add one of the climate contribution packages directly during your flight booking or afterwards via My trip.

The following section explains the proportions of the climate contribution in the respective packages that are allocated to three selected climate protection projects and the use of Sustainable Aviation Fuel (SAF):

Climate contribution 50 kg CO₂: ≈ 80% climate projects, ≈ 20% SAF

Climate contribution 100 kg CO₂: ≈ 85% climate projects, ≈ 15% SAF

Climate contribution 150 kg CO₂: ≈ 87% climate projects, ≈ 13% SAF

Climate contribution 200 kg CO₂: ≈ 87.5% climate projects, ≈ 12.5% SAF

Climate contribution 250 kg CO₂: ≈ 88% climate projects, ≈ 12% SAF

Climate contribution 400 kg CO₂: ≈ 87.5% climate projects, ≈ 12.5% SAF

Climate contribution 500 kg CO₂: ≈ 88% climate projects, ≈ 12% SAF

Climate contribution 600 kg CO₂: ≈ 88% climate projects, ≈ 12% SAF

What is Sustainable Aviation Fuel (SAF)?

Sustainable Aviation Fuel – SAF for short – is the umbrella term for sustainable aviation fuels. They can reduce lifecycle CO₂ emissions by up to 80 percent compared to fossil kerosene (Source: SAF: Aviation Fuel | Moeve).

SAF is produced from waste such as used cooking oil, plant residues or biomass without the use of fossil raw materials such as petroleum – materials that do not compete with food production. In addition to SAF from residual materials, electricity-based Power-to-Liquid fuels are also in development, also referred to as PtL or eSAF. For use in aviation, SAF is blended with conventional kerosene. One of the advantages of SAF as a "drop-in fuel" is that the existing infrastructure can be used without any issues.

Find out here how you can contribute to increasing the future use of SAF with the Condor Choice Fare.

Why is it important?

Alternative fuels are an important building block for reducing greenhouse gas emissions in aviation while using the existing aircraft fleet and infrastructure. As part of its Choice Fare, Condor purchases SAF and uses it on future Condor flights. These SAF volumes go beyond the quantities required by law.

Moreover, according to the German Aerospace Center (DLR), Sustainable Aviation Fuel (SAF) can help reduce contrails and climate impacts in aviation. Because SAF contains fewer aromatic compounds than kerosene, it results in fewer soot particles. This reduces, for example, the formation of ice crystals and thus the formation of cirrus clouds, which contribute to global warming.

title: Sustainable Aviation Fuel: From Climate Imperative To Strategic Asset | Aerospace Defense Outlook
authors: Dr.Ulrike Ziegler, President, Impact on Sustainable Aviation, Dr.Ulrike Ziegler, Impact on Sustainable Aviation
description:

Countries with access to sustainable feedstocks or renewable power will be able to develop strategic advantages in future aviation fuel markets.
